activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: Ontario combines the federal GST with its provincial sales tax into a single 13 percent Harmonized Sales Tax, shown as one HST line on receipts.
story:
Cohen opened his laptop at the kitchen table before his mother left for her shift, because she had said, casually and then not casually at all, that he should file his own taxes this year. He had a folder beside him, thin but real: four pay stubs from the hardware store, a T4 slip in an envelope he hadn't yet torn open, and a restaurant receipt from Friday night that he was keeping for a reason he couldn't entirely defend.

"It's due at the end of the month," his mother said, pulling on her jacket. "There's software that walks you through it. Don't guess."

"I never guess," he said, and she gave him a look that had survived eighteen years of use.

When the door closed he logged in and started with the pay stubs, lining them up chronologically the way he lined up anything he wanted to understand. The first thing he noticed was that the number at the top, the gross pay, was not the number that had landed in his bank account. Below the gross sat a short ladder of deductions: federal income tax, provincial income tax, Canada Pension Plan, Employment Insurance. Each one small, each one real, and together they took a bite he had never actually measured. He added up four months of deductions on paper and stared at the total. It was less than a video game console, which felt both trivial and enormous, depending on which way he looked at it, and he could not decide which way was honest.

His phone buzzed. Trinity had sent a photo of a bill from the Thai place near school, with the message: "why is there only ONE tax on this. cara says we got scammed. settle it."

Cohen enlarged the photo. At the bottom, under the pad thai and the spring rolls, a single line read HST, thirteen percent of the subtotal, one number, no separate federal and provincial charges. He typed back that it looked normal to him, then deleted that, because he wasn't sure it was true. He remembered receipts from when he was younger, or thought he did, with two tax lines. Or he remembered Americans' receipts from movies. He genuinely could not place the memory, and it bothered him the way a wrong note bothers someone who can almost play the piece.

"Hold on," he typed. "Calling you."

Trinity answered on speaker, Cara audible behind her, still arguing that restaurants in Toronto were skimming by hiding a tax. "Everywhere else has two," Cara said. "Federal and provincial. Everyone knows that."

"That's the thing," Cohen said. "I don't think everyone knows that. I think Ontario has the Harmonized Sales Tax." He heard himself say the word Harmonized and liked the shape of it, though he wouldn't have admitted that. "One tax. Thirteen percent. The GST and the provincial tax combined, so it shows as a single HST line."

"Where did you read that?"

"Nowhere yet. Give me a second." He put the phone on the table, opened a browser, and found the Ontario government page confirming it while Trinity and Cara bickered about whether spring rolls had been twenty cents cheaper last year. He read the line twice. "Okay. Confirmed. One tax line. Thirteen percent. You weren't scammed."

Cara made a sound of grudging concession. "Then why did my uncle's bill in Montreal look different?"

"That I can't tell you," Cohen said, and meant it. He was aware that his certainty had a small perimeter and that beyond it was a country of tax regimes he knew nothing about.

He hung up and returned to the T4, which summarized the year the pay stubs had promised: box 14, his total income, then the deducted income tax, the CPP, the EI, each figure corresponding to a line he'd already met. The software, when he entered everything, asked patient questions and then showed him a number. He was getting money back. A refund. He sat with that for a minute, because his first instinct was triumph, and his second was a suspicion of his own triumph. The government had taken more than it turned out to want, and now it was returning the difference, and he could not decide whether that was a fair system working or an awkward one stumbling into fairness. He thought of Mr. Harper, his law teacher, who liked to say that most disputes about money were really disputes about what counts as yours. Cohen had written that down in September and understood it only now, at the kitchen table, in a small way.

Trinity texted again: a photo of the bill torn in half, then the words "cara's paying her half in cash, exact change, no tip. explain tax to her again."

Cohen laughed once, out loud, alone in the kitchen. He screenshotted his refund number, then closed the file without sending it to anyone, because it was his, whatever that meant. He texted Trinity: "Tell Cara the thirteen percent was legitimate. The tip is between her and her conscience."

He looked at the receipt from Friday night still sitting in the folder, one HST line along the bottom, and slipped it back under the T4 for next year.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The US federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, though many states and cities set a higher minimum.
story:
Megan filled out the application at the kitchen table on a Tuesday, her laptop propped against the cereal box because the hinge was broken. The job was at a sandwich shop four blocks from her house, the one with the green awning and the poster that said NOW HIRING, and the form wanted her hourly expectations, which she left blank because she did not know what to expect. Her mother leaned over her shoulder on the way to the sink and said, "Anything's more than nothing," and Megan typed in seven twenty-five, because she had heard that number somewhere, maybe from a cousin, maybe from the internet, and it sounded official.

They called her that same night. The manager asked if she could start Saturday at nine and she said yes before she had checked whether she was free, then texted Aisha in capitals: I GOT IT. Aisha texted back a row of exclamation points and then, a few minutes later, the detail that Megan would turn over for the rest of the week: Aisha had also been hired, at a smoothie place in the mall, but her mall was across the state line, forty minutes away, where her father had moved in the spring.

On Saturday Megan learned the register, the bread knife, and the correct way to wipe down the slicer, which the shift lead demonstrated twice because Megan's hands were shaking slightly, though not from fear. By the end of her shift her feet ached in a way she suspected would debilitate her by the following weekend, and she had earned, according to her own arithmetic in the bus shelter, fifty-one dollars and something, before taxes, which the paycheck would reveal in two weeks and which she was already dividing among a phone screen, a contribution to her mother, and the savings account her grandmother kept mentioning.

Aisha came over Sunday with her own arithmetic, printed on actual receipt paper because Aisha liked paper, and they spread it on the living room floor between them like a map. "Nine seventy," Aisha said, tapping the line. "Per hour. Same hours as you, roughly, same kind of work, yours is even harder, you have a bread knife."

Megan looked at her own projected number, which she had written on the corner of an envelope. Seven twenty-five. She turned the envelope over as though the other side might have a different answer. "That can't be right," she said. "You're sixteen. I'm sixteen. It's the same country, Aisha."

They took the problem to Helena, who was doing homework on Megan's porch and who believed, as a matter of principle, that every confusing thing could be solved by reading. Helena looked it up on her phone while Megan's little brother threw an arboreal collection of sticks at the oak in the yard, pretending they were spears, and Helena read silently for a while, which was her way of building suspense.

"The federal minimum wage is seven twenty-five an hour," Helena said at last. "And it's been seven twenty-five since July 24, 2009."

"Since when," Megan said.

"Two thousand nine. But states can set a higher minimum, and some cities too. That's why Aisha's is nine seventy. She's across the line."

Aisha sat back on her heels. "So the country says one thing, and then everyone just decides whether to listen?"

"More or less," Helena said, and went back to her homework, because for Helena the matter was now closed, a fact located and pinned, whereas for Megan it had just opened. She thought about it while she made peanut butter toast for her brother, cutting it diagonally the way he required, and she thought about it in the shower, and the thinking had that texture her father called metaphysics when he wanted to tease her, though her father was not here to tease anyone, which was a separate ache she filed away.

On one hand, the rule had to be simple and it had to be the same everywhere, because otherwise what was a country for, and because Aisha's smoothies and Megan's sandwiches were the same work, worth the same sweat. On the other hand, the town four blocks from Megan's house was not the same town at all; rents differed, bus fares differed, and Aisha's mall sat in a place that had apparently decided its floor should be higher, and who was Megan, who had never paid rent, to say the floor was wrong? She could hold both ideas, and she noticed that holding both made her slower to be angry, which felt like growing up and also like losing something quick and clean.

What she could not do was pretend the difference away. She texted Aisha on Wednesday: are you still doing the bus both ways. Aisha said yes, forty minutes each direction, and Megan, who had been hoarding her first check in her head, opened the banking app her mother had set up for her and moved some of it into a folder labeled Aisha's birthday, which was not for months, which gave her time to think of a story that would let Aisha accept it.

Two Fridays later the envelope came, thin as a leaf. Megan opened it at the kitchen table while her mother watched from the doorway without pretending not to. The number was less than the number in her head, because taxes, because the two hours she had been sent home early on a slow Tuesday, and she sat with it for a moment before she texted Aisha a photograph and one line: "same country." Aisha sent back a photograph of her own check, and beneath it, "bring the envelope next time, we're doing the math right."

Megan's mother set a mug of tea down beside her and said, "How was it, the first one?"

"Small," Megan said. "But mine."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross introduced the five stages of denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance in her 1969 book On Death and Dying, originally to describe terminally ill patients facing their own death.
story:
Austin had been standing at the edge of the graveside chairs for eleven minutes, and in all that time he had not once thought about the five stages, which was the problem.

He had expected to think about them. Ms. Anderson had brought them up in health class back in October, back when his grandfather was still shuffling to the mailbox in his cracked loafers. Denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance. Everyone in class had nodded as though these were stations on a train line, as though grief were a matter of buying a ticket and riding through. Now the service was ending, the pastor folding her notes, and Austin had felt none of it. He felt like a coatroom attendant, handing out hugging and thank-yous and yes-he-was-a-great-man to relatives whose names he half remembered.

Cheyenne appeared at his elbow holding two paper cups of lemonade she had smuggled from the reception tent. She did not say sorry for your loss, which was the first kind thing anyone had done for him all morning.

"Nothing's happening to me," he said. "Everyone's crying and I'm just standing here. I keep checking, like, am I in denial? I don't think so."

"My mom kept asking me that after my grandfather," Cheyenne said. She looked out across the rows of headstones instead of at him. "Which stage are you in, honey. As if I could tell her." She pressed a cup into his hand. "Then Helena made me look it up, and honestly it helped. Those stages, the five of them, Kübler-Ross wrote them in 1969, in her book On Death and Dying, and she wasn't writing about people like us at all. She was describing her own terminally ill patients, dying people facing their own deaths. Not mourners. Not grandchildren at funerals."

Austin turned that over while a great-aunt nearby blew her nose with the force of a trumpet. "So we've been grading ourselves against a test written for somebody else."

"Basically." Cheyenne shrugged, and the shrug had a whole year of her own grandfather in it. "Ms. Anderson never mentioned that part. She made it sound like the weather. You will pass through anger on Tuesday."

The reception tent had folding tables with casseroles and a photo board, and Austin's mother wanted him to stand beside it and receive condolences, which he did, for forty minutes, while his younger cousins grew obstreperous near the punch bowl and had to be extracted by an uncle. Between well-wishers he kept returning to what Cheyenne had said. He tried it against himself like a new pair of shoes. He was not in denial, but he did notice that this morning, dressing, he had chosen the tie his grandfather gave him and had thought, briefly, that the old man would be pleased, in the present tense, before correcting it. He was not angry either, though when a second cousin called Pop a character, some small heat rose in him, a wish to defend the man from being denigrated into a joke, reduced to a fond anecdote by people who had only known him at holidays. Maybe that was anger. Maybe it was just love wearing its coat buttoned wrong.

He found Helena outside the tent, sitting on the low stone wall that separated the cemetery from the county road, a highway so ordinary that trucks went by without slowing, hauling gravel to somewhere that had nothing to do with any of this.

"Cheyenne told you," Helena said, not a question.

"About the book. 1969, her own patients, facing their own dying." He sat down on the wall, which was cold through his dress pants. "I don't know whether that makes me feel better or worse. Like I've been handed back a blank page and told good luck."

"Both," Helena said. "It's always both." She picked at the lichen on the stone. "My grandmother's hospice nurse used to say the stages were a map of one country, and we were all standing in a different one. I thought that was wise at the time. Now I think she just liked sounding wise."

He laughed for the first time in six days, a strange bark that startled a grackle off a headstone. It felt disloyal and necessary at once. His grandfather would have laughed too; the old man had treated every doctor, pastor and banker in town with the same amused skepticism, as though authority of any kind were a despot to be tolerated rather than obeyed, and Austin had inherited the habit without ever deciding to.

They walked back across the grass together, the three of them, and at the graveside the flowers were already wilting in the heat, the edges of the ribbons gone soft. The dirt beside the vault had been covered with a green carpet so no one would have to look at it, which struck Austin now as its own kind of denial, a small one, harmless, maybe even kind. He stood where the chairs had been and tried to say something inward, a goodbye, and what came instead was the memory of July, the two of them splitting a gas station lemonade on the tailgate, his grandfather saying the sky that evening looked like a bruise deciding to heal. He did not know which stage that was. He suspected it was none of them, or all of them shuffled together, or a country Kübler-Ross had never mapped because she was busy with her dying patients, describing what she saw honestly, and the rest of them had borrowed it and worn it wrong for fifty years.

His mother called from the cars. He took one last look at the flowers, then bent and picked up a small stone from the edge of the path, smoothed by old rain, and set it on the corner of the plot where the grass would eventually come.

"For the drive home," he said to no one, and put his hands in his pockets and went.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Aristotle named three means of persuasion: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, the logic of the argument.
story:
The topic was posted on Tuesday outside Room 114: school start times should move an hour later, and the debate, for anyone in third-year Spanish, had to run five minutes entirely in that language. Jonathan signed his name to the list because Leila had signed hers, and because he had learned, over three years of sitting beside her in class, that her ambitions had a way of reorganizing his own. She wanted to argue the affirmative. He took the negative so they could practice against each other, and because he privately thought the negative was the harder side and he wanted, for once, to be the perspicacious one.

He built his case in a notebook over two evenings, working at the kitchen table while his mother washed dishes. Demora, he wrote, delay. The buses would need new routes; younger siblings would wait alone in the dark; sports practices would end after sunset. He numbered his points and numbered the sub-points beneath them, and each one was a reason, cleanly stated, that a reasonable person could not easily refuse. On Thursday he read the list to Leila in the hallway, translating as he went, and she listened with her chin in her hand.

"Suena como una calculadora," she said. It sounds like a calculator.

"What else is there?"

She shrugged and pushed through the door of Mr. Andersen's room, where the desks had been shoved into a rough horseshoe for the practice round. Mr. Andersen, who taught the class and coached the debate team in the fall, sat at the side with a stopwatch and a legal pad and said almost nothing, which was his method.

Kara went first, on the affirmative, and her Spanish was plainer than Jonathan's but she told a story: a girl she knew who took two buses at six in the morning and slept through first period anyway, whose grades rose the one term her mother drove her. When she finished, Mr. Andersen clicked the stopwatch and said, "Three and a half minutes. Add something." Kara said she would add another story.

Jonathan went second, and his five minutes held, and his grammar held, and when he sat down he understood before anyone spoke that something had not held. The room had been polite the way a room is polite during long division. Leila was looking at him with the particular patience she saved for his blind spots.

"You know he has that chart," she said afterward, in the parking lot, unwrapping a granola bar. "The one he made for the debate team. Aristotle, three means of persuasion. Ethos, pathos, logos. It's taped inside his clipboard."

"I know the words."

"Then why was your whole speech one of them?"

Jonathan took the clipboard idea as permission and, before school on Friday, looked at the chart himself, tacked up in the team room beside the trophy shelf. Ethos, the speaker's credibility. Pathos, the audience's emotions. Logos, the logic of the argument. Aristotle had named three means of persuasion, and the chart drew them as three doors, and Jonathan stood there realizing he had spent two evenings decorating one door and calling it a house. Every point so far had been only logos, and in a language he was still learning, logos arrived thin, every clause a small effort, none of it carrying the ease that makes an audience trust a speaker rather than merely follow one.

He did not want to fake pathos; that felt like cheating, and the distrust between manipulation and persuasion was exactly the kind of thing he could not yet name in Spanish. But the dialectic between his position and Kara's, the way each argument pressed against the other until something sturdier stood between them, had produced an honest middle he had not noticed: he did not actually believe start times should stay the same; he believed they should move later for the high school only, and he could say why with his own experience, which was ethos of a kind, the credibility of someone who lived the schedule he was defending. He rewrote the speech Saturday morning with one story of his own near the beginning, his sister waiting for him at the corner in November dark, and kept the numbered reasons after, fewer now, chosen rather than accumulated.

On Monday he gave it, and the room was not polite. Kara leaned forward during the story and sat back during the reasons, and when the five minutes ended, before Mr. Andersen could speak, Leila said quietly, "Eso." That. Jonathan folded his notes in half and felt the fold under his thumb. Leila was next at the podium, and she began, in Spanish, "Mi opponent, whom I respect..."

He watched her, listening for which door she would open first.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The derivative of a constant is zero, so adding 7 to a function shifts its graph up but leaves its derivative unchanged.
story:
The tutoring centre smelled of dry-erase markers and the burnt coffee Ms. Khoury kept warming on the counter beside the sign-in sheets. Addison signed in at four, took her usual table by the window, and set out her worksheet on derivatives, the one she'd been avoiding since Sunday. At the next table, Genesis had the same worksheet, folded into quarters and flattened again, which meant she'd been carrying it around unhappily for days too.

"Question four," Genesis said, without greeting. "The height of a ball or a rocket or whatever it is. Did you get a maximum at three seconds?"

"I don't have a maximum yet," Addison said. "I have a derivative and a bad feeling."

They compared functions. Genesis had written h of t equals negative t squared plus six t, and Addison had written the same thing plus seven, because the problem had said the launch platform was seven metres tall, and Addison had added it to the height. Their derivatives came out identical: negative two t plus six. Genesis looked at Addison's page and then at her own, circumspect, the way she was before accusing anyone of anything.

"Yours is wrong," Genesis said finally. "You added the seven. Now our derivatives match and one of us definitely messed up, because different functions can't have the same derivative."

"Can't they?" Addison turned her pencil over and erased nothing, just held it. She graphed her function quickly, the parabola opening downward, and slid it across the table. Genesis graphed hers beside it. The curves were the same shape, the same width, tipping over at the same point. Addison's sat exactly seven units higher, like Genesis's graph lifted by an invisible shelf.

"Three seconds," Genesis said, pointing at both peaks. "Both of us. Even with your seven." She sat back. "The derivative of a constant is zero. That's why. It just dies."

"So I didn't mess up." Addison heard how defensive it came out and laughed at herself. Across the room, a younger kid asked Ms. Khoury why atoms ionize when metals are heated, and Ms. Khoury began pulling a hand-cranked demo from the supply shelf, so the next few minutes smelled faintly of ozone and metal shavings.

The centre ran in quiet strata: the little kids with flashcards at the front, the middle-schoolers in the middle, and the calculus stragglers at the window tables, where the work was lonelier even with company. Addison had been signed up since October because she was failing pre-calculus and had told her mother, in the car, that math was a language she had stopped being able to hear. She hadn't said the second part out loud since.

That evening she texted Aila, who had finished the worksheet days ago, from the waiting area while her mother idled outside in the pickup lane. "So adding 7 to the function shifts the whole graph up but leaves the derivative exactly the same," she typed. "Genesis and I spent an hour arguing about who was wrong before we realized neither of us was. Is that a real rule or a coincidence?"

Aila's reply took six minutes, long enough that Addison watched the taillights of the car ahead and rehearsed an apology for asking something obvious. Then the message came: "Real rule. Constants don't matter to the slope. Feel free to be smug about it." Addison grinned at the screen and typed back, "Too late," and her mother leaned over and honked the horn once, gently, meaning let's go.

The next session, Ms. Khoury put a new worksheet in front of her, profit functions this time, a company deciding how much of something to make. "Find where the profit peaks," Ms. Khoury said, and moved on to Genesis, who was erasing half a page. Addison read the problem twice. The function had a constant in it, some fixed cost or fee, and she looked at it for a moment before deciding it could wait until after she'd found the derivative, since it would die anyway.

She worked through the algebra in the window light, checking each line the way she now knew to, not skimming. When she set the derivative equal to zero and solved, the answer came out clean, a whole number of units, a maximum she believed in. She drew a small arrow at the peak of the graph and wrote three seconds next to nothing, out of habit, then crossed it out and wrote the actual answer, and underlined it twice.

"How many units?" Genesis asked from the next table, not looking up.

"Forty," Addison said. "You?"

"Forty," said Genesis, and they both turned back to their pages.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The 1930s Dust Bowl followed the plowing of the Great Plains' native deep-rooted grasses, which had held the soil, so when drought came the wind carried the topsoil away.
story:
The wind had been blowing for six days, and by Wednesday the top layer of Kaylee's plot had begun to move. She stood at the chain-link fence of the community garden with her hands in her jacket pockets and watched a thin brown ribbon of soil lift off the far beds and stream between the tomato stakes like water finding a channel. The fence, she had long since habituated herself to its gaps and its sag, was not much of a deterrence against anything, not the wind, not the kids who cut through at night, not the dumping. Someone had left a broken dresser beside the lettuce again. She dragged it to the curb and went back to staring at her soil, which was leaving.

The garden sat on a city-owned lot at the corner of Felton and Ninth, and in April the council had voted to sell it. The vote had been quiet, a line item in a budget meeting, and by the time the gardeners found out, the sale was already scheduled for August. Ms. Cruz, who had run the garden for eleven years and kept the shed locked and the water bill in a folder with her name on it, had told them not to bother fighting it. "We can still get a harvest," she said. "Plant fast, harvest early, and be done before the bulldozers."

Kaylee had a different problem than the bulldozers. Her soil was going now, in June, before anything was ripe. The spring had been dry, and the plots at the garden had always been tilled edge to edge, every gardener turning the whole rectangle of ground each spring because that was how her grandmother had taught her, bare soil from fence to fence, clean and ready. She had done the same thing. Now she crouched and pressed her fingers into the surface and found it loose as ash, and beneath it, where the seeds were, ground gone hard and dry.

Knox showed up after school with two bottles of Gatorade and no plan, which was usual. He walked the beds with her, and they stood a long time at the corner where the wind came in hardest. "It's like a beach," he said. "Loose sand, no roots, everything shifts." Kaylee said nothing, because something was assembling itself in her head, half remembered. In October, before the sale was announced, her environmental science class had gone to a farm two counties over, and the farmer had walked them along the edge of her fields where she left wide strips of grass unplowed between the rows of soy. Kaylee had been half asleep on the bus and had not written it down, and the farmer had talked about soil and roots and holding while the wind pulled at her hat, and Kaylee had filed it away as a nice morning.

That night she dug out her textbook and found the chapter, and read it twice, and sat with her laptop open until almost midnight. The Great Plains, before the 1930s, had been covered in native grasses, deep-rooted, and those roots had held the soil. Then the grasses were plowed under for farmland. When the drought came, there was nothing left to hold the ground, and the wind carried the topsoil away. She read the name of it once, then again. The next morning she found Knox at his locker. "Those strips of grass at that farm," she said. "Remember them?" Knox squinted. "The ones she never plowed? Vaguely." "It's the Dust Bowl," she said. "That's why she left the grass. Roots hold soil." Knox closed his locker slowly. "We're not the Dust Bowl." "We're a small dry windy lot with no roots and no rain and a deadline."

They asked Ms. Cruz for seed, and Ms. Cruz, who did not ask why, gave them the dusty jar of annual rye from the shed and the wheelbarrow and, grudgingly, the hose. On Saturday Felicia came too, and by afternoon the three of them had sown a four-foot band of rye along the windward fence and narrower bands between the beds, tamping the seed in with their shoes. The germination was thin and slow in the drought, but it came, pale green threads in the brown, and within two weeks Kaylee could kneel at the border and see the difference herself: on the garden side of the young grass the soil had stopped moving, collecting in a low soft drift against the stems instead of streaming through them. The beds inside the bands held their moisture longer into the afternoon. Her tomatoes, which had been going yellow and slack, stiffened.

The council's buyer came in late July, a man in a gray car who walked the lot with a clipboard while Ms. Cruz trailed him saying nothing. He stopped at the grass strips. "What's this?" "A windbreak," Ms. Cruz said. "We had erosion." He looked at the tomatoes, the peppers, the new drifts of soil lying still, and Kaylee, who was weeding nearby and pretending not to listen, heard him say the word "improvement" to himself as he wrote something down. She did not know what it meant. Maybe nothing. The sale could still go through in August, the lot could still be paved, and a strip of rye was not a counterargument to a budget shortfall. She was honest with herself about that, kneeling there with dirt under her nails. All she knew for certain was that the soil had been leaving and now it was staying, and the tomatoes were ripening, and something green was holding where nothing had held before.

On the last Saturday of July they harvested everything at once, ahead of any deadline, and carried boxes of tomatoes across town to the pantry on Felton Street. Felicia balanced a box on her hip and knocked on the door with her elbow. A woman opened it, looked at the boxes, and said, "You grew these?" "In the ground," Kaylee said. "With the wind coming at it." She set her box down on the step, then went back for the next one.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: An authentic cadence, a V chord moving to the I chord, sounds final, which is why melodies usually end their last phrase with it.
story:
The church hall smelled of floor polish and the cold remnants of Sunday coffee, and Victoria had claimed the corner by the piano because the light from the stained glass window fell across the music stand there, turning her blank staff paper faintly blue and gold. She had four bars finished. Twelve empty bars waited below them like unpainted rooms in a house she was supposed to live in by Friday.

The assignment had come from Mr. Yip, who taught theory on Thursday evenings in the basement for whoever showed up. Sixteen bars, chord changes, proper notation, and no borrowing anyone else's tune. "You can commodify anything these days," he had said last week, holding up a phone playing an ad that used a mangled Chopin waltz. "Even grief, even joy. But a melody you write yourself, on paper, belongs to you until you decide otherwise." Victoria had thought the line was a little theatrical, but she had also written it in the margin of her notebook.

Mae arrived first, unwinding a scarf, then Maika, who carried a guitar case even though he never played during these sessions. They had until six o'clock, when the evening service would need the hall back. Victoria played her four bars for them, twice through.

"It's pretty," Mae said, which was the kind of sentence that could mean anything.

"It doesn't go anywhere." Victoria rested her hands in her lap. "Or it goes somewhere and then stops being shy about nothing. I don't know. I have the chords for the first phrase, G to C to Am, but after that I keep circling."

Maika leaned over the page. "You're an autodidact when it comes to this part, right? You taught yourself piano off YouTube before Mr. Yip's class. My cousin's the same. You learn fast but you skip the boring grammar." He said it without cruelty, the way he said most things, and Victoria admitted to herself that he was right: she could play anything put in front of her, but building from nothing was a different muscle, one she had never trained.

She worked through the middle eight bars slowly, hunting and peking, crossing out, rewriting. Mae sat on the floor with her theory homework, occasionally calling out a note name she was unsure of, and Maika hummed the bass line Victoria pointed at, his low voice filling the corner of the hall like furniture being moved in. By quarter to six she had sixteen bars, complete, notated, with the chords pencilled above the staves. She played the whole thing start to finish.

At the end, Mae frowned.

"What," Victoria said.

"It doesn't sound finished. Like it's over, but it doesn't sound finished. Is that a thing that can happen?"

Victoria played the last phrase again, listening harder this time. The final two chords were a D minor moving to a G, and then she had simply stopped. The melody sounded like a person walking out of a room mid-sentence. She turned to the page and tried the last bar an octave up, then an octave down, and the unfinished feeling followed the notes whichever way they went.

Mr. Yip came up from the basement with his coat already on, keys in hand. He did not say anything about cadences. He looked at her page, hummed her final phrase once, quiet, and said only, "You solved the middle section. That was the hard part." Then he waited by the door while Mae packed up, which meant he had decided to say nothing more, which meant Victoria had to find it herself or not.

She stayed at the piano after Mae and Maika went out into the dark, and she thought about every melody she had ever played that did sound finished. Hymns, mostly, ones she had played for the Sunday services since she was twelve. She pulled the hymnal from the shelf under the piano and turned to the last lines of a dozen of them, playing only the endings. In nearly every one, the same thing happened: the chord built on the fifth note of the scale, then the chord built on the first. G to C, in the key of C. She played that movement by itself and felt the floor settle under her, the sound closing like a door.

Maika had come back for his scarf, forgotten over a chair. He watched her play it three times.

"That's the authentic cadence," he said. "Mae's cousin rambles about it. The five chord going to the one. It's why the ends of songs sound like ends."

"The V chord going to the I chord," Victoria said, mostly to fix it in her mind, and she wrote the letters above her final bar, V, then I, and changed her last melody note so it landed on the tonic, and the phrase gathered itself in and came to rest.

She was not sanguine about the whole thing, though. She played the sixteen bars once more and heard, underneath the satisfying close, all the bars in the middle that she had chosen out of tiredness rather than conviction, places where she had taken the easy chord because it was near her hand. She could keep them or open everything back up, and Friday was two days away. Mae's frown had been a kind of gift, but it had also been a door she could not close again; she would hear the difference now in every ending, forever.

The stained glass had gone grey with the evening. Mr. Yip's keys jingled somewhere near the vestibule, patient, and Victoria took out a fresh eraser and held it above the ninth bar.

"Just the ninth," she said to the empty hall. "Just the ninth, and then I stop."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: German capitalizes every noun, not only names, which helps a reader of a German article spot the nouns in a sentence at a glance.
story:
Alicia had chosen German for exactly the wrong reasons, and she knew it. In grade ten she had picked it over Spanish because the class was smaller and the timetable was easier, and now, three years later, she sat in the school library with a photocopied news article in front of her, three paragraphs of it, and a summary she was supposed to deliver aloud to Ms. Rajapakse at four o'clock. The article was about a small town debating whether to close its swimming pool. She had a dictionary, a pencil, and fifty minutes.

Julianna was already there, at the corner table by the windows, headphones around her neck, working on something for chemistry. She looked up when Alicia dropped her bag. "Is that the German thing? For Rajapakse?"

"Three paragraphs, summarize aloud, in German." Alicia sat down and flattened the photocopy. "She said it doesn't have to be perfect. It has to be mine."

"That's her whole thing," Julianna said. "She said the same thing about the French oral last year. She wants your own words, not the article's words wearing a fake moustache."

Alicia began with the first sentence, and almost immediately the capitals defeated her. Word after word began with a big letter, not only at the start of a sentence, and she could not tell which of them were names she should look up and which were ordinary words she was somehow supposed to know. She circled them, one after another, and the page began to look like a field of small suns. She was halfway through looking up the third one, finding it meant "budget," a plain ordinary word, when Jeremie slid into the seat across from her with his own photocopy, the same article.

"Yours doing it too?" he asked. "All the capitals."

"Everywhere. I thought I'd found the mayor's name four times and it turns out to be the word for council."

Julianna pulled one headphone off. "In German," she said, "capitalizes every noun, not only names." She said it the way she said things she'd read once and kept, and went back to her chemistry.

Alicia looked at the sentence again, and it reorganized itself in front of her. It wasn't random decoration. Every capitalized word was a noun; the nouns stood out at a glance, the way a fence stands out in a field once you know to look for the fence and not for the individual posts. She went through the first paragraph and underlined every capital that wasn't at a sentence start, and there they were, the skeleton of the sentence, the things the sentence was actually about: the town, the pool, the money, the summer. The small words in between, the lower-case ones, were mostly holding it together. She had been reading German like English, hunting for meaning word by word, when the language was handing her the nouns first, like a waiter setting down the main dish before the sides.

"Wait," Jeremie said, watching her. "Show me that." He took his own copy and did the same thing, and for a while they worked in a silence broken only by the dictionary's pages and Julianna's pen.

The second paragraph was harder, because knowing the nouns was not the same as knowing what happened. The council had voted, or had been voted about; Alicia could not tell which, and the dictionary offered both directions without any opinion. This was the part she had always hated, the part that had made her feel, in a visceral way she was embarrassed to remember, that she was simply not a languages person and had been pretending for three years. In grade eleven she had nearly asked her mother to write a note transferring her out. Her mother had said it was her choice. Alicia had chosen to stay, partly out of stubbornness, partly because quitting felt like admitting she had wasted two years, and she had never quite decided which motive had been the real one. Maybe an egoist stays because leaving looks like a confession, she thought, and maybe a stubborn person does, and maybe there's no difference that matters.

She built her summary the way Ms. Rajapakse had taught them, in the target language, short sentences, no dictionary on her lap when she spoke it. "The town has a pool. The pool costs money. The council will decide in the summer." She said it under her breath, twice, feeling the sentences as objects, small and complete.

At ten to four, Jeremie tested her, holding the article and asking questions in English that she had to answer in German, and she got through it with two stumbles and one word she had to say in English and translate with her hands, drawing a rectangle in the air until Julianna said "pool" without looking up. Then it was time, and Alicia walked to the far side of the library where Ms. Rajapakse waited at the desk by the periodicals.

Alicia laid the article face down, the way she'd been told to, and began. Her voice caught once, on the word for decided, and she heard herself slow down instead of rush past it, which was new. The summary came out shorter than the article and slightly wrong in at least one place, she could feel it, something about who wanted the pool kept open, the residents or the newspaper, and she said so, out loud, in German, "I am not sure here," and then she finished.

Ms. Rajapakse wrote something in her book, and then she turned the article over and set it beside Alicia's underlined copy, capitals picked out all down the margin like streetlights.

"Tell me," she said, "why you circled these."

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A statistically significant result can still be a tiny effect: with a very large sample, even a difference too small to matter in practice can pass the significance test.
story:
Violet spread the two articles across the kitchen table, weighting the corners with the salt shaker and her mother's mug of cold coffee. One was by Dr. Salim, arguing that students who texted frequently showed lower scores on a reading comprehension measure. The other, by a team from another university, found the opposite: no meaningful difference between heavy texters and light texters at all. Mr. Qureshi had assigned them the same question on purpose, and he wanted a critical review by Friday, not a summary. Violet had read both twice on the bus and understood almost nothing the second time.

Her phone buzzed against the wood. It was Kenneth, whose essay on the same pair of articles was due in the same class. "Are you going with the first one?" he had texted. "Salim's got the statistically significant result. That's the winner, right?" She typed back that she didn't know yet, then set the phone face down, because she suspected the answer was not that simple, and she didn't want to borrow his certainty before she'd earned her own.

She pulled Salim's article closer and found the results table again. The heavy texters had scored lower, and the difference was flagged as significant. That word had sounded grandiose to her all week, like a judge's gavel coming down. Then she turned to the methods section and did what Mr. Qureshi kept telling them to do in every class: check the sample. Salim had tested nearly forty thousand students. The number sat there on the page, ordinary and enormous at once. She frowned at it, chewing the end of her pen.

Kadence arrived at four with her backpack and half a loaf of banana bread, having texted that she was coming to work and not to argue about it. She flopped into the other chair and stole a corner of the bread Violet's mother had left under a towel. "I don't even know what I'm supposed to be critical of," Kadence said, mouth full. "One says yes, one says no. Someone's wrong."

"Or both are right," Violet said slowly, "about different things." She slid the first article across. "Look at the actual scores. The heavy texters averaged, like, a hair below the others. The difference wouldn't matter to anyone." She tapped the page. "But he tested so many people that it came out significant anyway."

Kadence leaned in, reading, her eyebrows climbing. "So significant doesn't mean big?"

"Apparently not with a sample that size." Violet heard the words leave her mouth and felt something click shut in her chest, the small satisfying latch of a fact fitting where a confusion had been. "A tiny effect can pass the test if your sample's huge. So his headline says one thing and his numbers say something quieter." She pulled the article back and underlined the table twice, hard enough that the pen tore a little.

The second article made a different kind of sense now. Its authors had tested a few hundred students, and they had written plainly that any difference too small to matter in practice wasn't worth reporting as a finding. Salim hadn't lied, exactly; he had leaned on the weight of the word significant while the effect itself was thin as onion skin. The other team had simply declined to make a big claim out of a small difference. Violet opened her laptop and began to type, and Kadence watched her go for a while, then started drafting her own essay on the other side of the bread plate.

When Kenneth texted again near dinnertime, Violet answered honestly: she was going to argue that the significant study and the null study weren't really disagreeing, that one had mistaken volume for weight, though she still wasn't sure how to say it without sounding like she was dismissing forty thousand students. She didn't know yet, she told him, whether that uncertainty belonged in the final paragraph or needed to be resolved first. She looked at the two articles, the light from the window going amber on their pages, and typed one more line at the bottom of her draft, unfinished, holding the place where the honest thing would go. Then she reached over and tore the last piece of banana bread in half.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: The Venona decrypts of Soviet intelligence messages, released by the US government in 1995, confirmed that Soviet spy networks had operated in the United States.
story:
Ryder had been assigned the two books in June, before freshman orientation even posted the reading list properly, and he had carried them to his grandfather's house because the house was quiet and the porch smelled like cedar and his grandfather left him alone for hours at a time. The assignment was simple in its wording and impossible in its execution: compare the historians' explanations of the Cold War against the evidence. One book argued that American fear of Soviet espionage had been inflated, a panic ginned up by politicians; the other argued the threat had been real and badly handled. Each wrote as though the other were not merely wrong but dishonest. Ryder sat with a legal pad on his knee and wondered how two people looking at the same fifty years could come away with different planets.

His grandfather, an epicure of canned peaches and black coffee who distrusted anything fancier, drifted past with his mug and paused at the stack of books on the wicker table. "Gaddis?" he said, tapping one cover. Then he tapped the other. "Schrecker. Huh." He didn't elaborate, which Ryder had learned was how his grandfather signaled that a subject had a history he wasn't going to hand over for free.

Aleeza came by on Thursday because she'd been assigned the same books and had texted him a photo of her own legal pad with the words HELP written across the top in capitals. She spread her notes on the porch boards and made her case first. "Schrecker says the spy fear was inflated. Gaddis says it wasn't. I like Schrecker's writing better. She eviscerates the other side. It's satisfying to read."

"Satisfying isn't evidence," Ryder said, and immediately felt like a jerk, because he had spent three days being satisfied by Gaddis for the mirror-image reason. "Sorry. I keep doing that too. I believe the one who writes better."

"So how do we decide anything?" Aleeza flopped back against the railing. "Is it just which voice we like?"

Mr. Chanthavong, the neighbor whose garden ran along the property line, was watering his tomatoes and had apparently been listening for longer than either of them realized. "When I was in college," he said, "we had a professor who told us a history book is a photograph of the historian as much as the history. Check when the photograph was taken." Then he went back to his tomatoes, which was his way, and Ryder sat there feeling something shift.

He went inside and pulled the publication dates. Schrecker's book: 1998. Gaddis's book: also late nineties. Both after the crucial date. But her argument leaned on earlier work, work she'd done in the eighties, and he sat on the porch steps tracing the chain of citation backward, book to book, until his finger stopped on a monograph from 1983 that her whole first chapter rested on. Nineteen eighty-three. Twelve years before something. He ran upstairs to the box of his grandfather's papers he'd noticed in the hall closet, the one he'd assumed was tax records, because his grandfather had once said, offhand, that he'd done cryptography work for the Army after the war and Ryder had filed it away as one of those things old men say.

The box was not tax records. It held folders of photocopies and a mimeographed summary with a cover sheet he read twice on the landing. The Venona decrypts of Soviet intelligence messages, released by the US government in 1995, confirmed that Soviet spy networks had operated in the United States. Ryder read it aloud to himself, then went down the stairs holding the page like it might tear.

"Grandpa. This monograph Schrecker builds on came out in 1983. The decrypts came out in 1995. She couldn't have seen them. He couldn't have seen them. The whole argument that the spying was exaggerated was written before anyone could check it against the messages." His grandfather took the page, read it without any surprise at all, and set it beside his peaches.

"I knew some of those decrypts before they were public," he said. "We weren't allowed to say. Half the country called it paranoia and the other half called it McCarthyism, and some days both halves were right, which is a thing your books won't tell you." He looked at Ryder with something that was not quite a smile. "You want lemon in that iced tea?"

Aleeza appeared in the doorway, having followed the conversation halfway through, holding her legal pad. "So which one do we argue for?" she asked.

"Both," Ryder said. "The spying was real, and the panic hurt people, and the timing of the evidence decides which book you can trust on which claim. It's not tautological, it's just messy." He pulled the 1983 monograph out of his bag and set it on the table next to the photocopies, side by side, two photographs of the same country taken twelve years apart. His grandfather went inside for the lemon.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: The AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio's Sustained Investigation section asks for 15 digital images and counts for 60 percent of the score.
story:
Wyatt had taped his plan above the drying rack like a wanted poster: ten paintings of his grandfather's hands, one per week until spring, and beneath the list, the phrase "ten is enough." He had chosen hands because they were the one subject he could draw without thinking, which was also, Mr. Murphy kept hinting, the problem. On Tuesday afternoon the art room smelled of turpentine and the radiator's burnt dust, and Wyatt was stretching his fourth canvas when Adriel dropped a stapled printout on his table.

"From the College Board site," Adriel said. "You said you were doing the AP thing. Read the part I circled."

Wyatt wiped his fingers and read. The Sustained Investigation section asked for fifteen digital images, not ten, and it counted for sixty percent of the score. He read it twice, then a third time, as though the number might renegotiate. "Fifteen," he said. "Sixty percent of the whole thing rides on it."

"So your ten is not enough," Adriel said, with the gentleness of someone delivering weather.

Wyatt sat down on the stool and looked at the taped list. Ten had felt like a real commitment when he'd made it, a number with weight, and now it looked like a fraction of a number with more weight. Jessy, who had been photographing her own pieces against the window for the digital images she would have to submit, wandered over with her phone still raised. "You didn't read the requirements before you planned a year of work?"

"I read the school's sheet," Wyatt said. "It said ten artworks, artist's statement, done by April." He pulled the crumpled handout from his folder and smoothed it on the table: Ms. somebody from the guidance office had typed it in September, tidy and wrong. The school wanted ten; the exam wanted fifteen images; those were not the same ask at all, and he had built his whole year on the smaller one.

"Fifteen images doesn't even mean fifteen paintings," Jessy said, turning her phone toward him. "See, this is a detail shot. This is the same piece at a different stage. The investigation itself is what they score, the thinking, so the images are evidence of it."

"Then I need more thinking," Wyatt said, and hated how it came out, like thinking was a chore he could add to the list.

Mr. Murphy, who had been watering the dead orchid he refused to throw away, came over and looked at the printout without touching it. "So what are you going to do?"

Wyatt started to say he'd just add five more hands, and stopped, because he could hear how thin it would be, five more of a thing he already knew how to do. The word hegemony had come up in English class that morning, some critic on the canon, and he didn't fully grasp the theory, but he understood the shape of it now: the tyranny of what you're already good at. Ten safe paintings would beguile anyone flipping through them, himself included, smooth and skillful and saying nothing new. His grandfather's hands were a subject. They were not yet an investigation. He had never once asked, on paper, why the hands held him, what the drawings were actually chasing.

"Detail shots," he said slowly. "The calluses. The way the left one curls since the stroke. I could zoom in, I could show the process, the underdrawings." He was talking faster now, pulling a fresh sheet of newsprint toward him. "But I don't know if fifteen images of one pair of hands is an investigation or just an obsession."

"That's the honest question," Mr. Murphy said, and went back to the orchid.

Wyatt unrolled a new canvas and penciled a quick grid, the motion somatic and sure, his hands knowing the ritual before his head did. He crossed out "ten is enough" on the taped list and wrote nothing in its place, because the right number wasn't the point anymore. Five more images meant five more weeks of late nights, and something else would have to be given up, though he hadn't yet decided what. Adriel leaned over his shoulder and read the requirements page again, out loud this time, fifteen and sixty, like a countdown.

"One more thing," Jessy said, gathering her phone and her bag. "Whatever you write in the artist's statement, don't pretend you planned all fifteen from the start."

Wyatt laughed once, a short, real sound, and began drawing the curled hand, this time from memory, larger than life.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Holding static stretches for a long time, about 60 seconds or more per muscle, right before explosive activity can briefly reduce strength and power, so many programs warm up with dynamic movement.
story:
Edouard spread the notebook flat on the picnic table, weighting the pages with two stones from the flowerbed so the wind couldn't take them. Behind him the coach's email glowed on his phone screen: every runner had to submit a personal training plan by Monday morning, seven days laid out with rest days marked and warm-ups described, or lose the chance to compete in the invitational. Six days to figure out what he actually believed about his own body.

Dawson arrived first, cleats dangling from his fingers, and read the notebook upside down while he ate a plum. "You've got Saturday as nothing," he said. "That's not a plan, that's a gap."

"That's a rest day," Edouard said. "Growth happens when you stop."

Samson came through the gate carrying his own crumpled attempt, a single page with more cross-outs than words, and dropped onto the grass. "Mine's garbage," he said cheerfully. "That's why I'm here. Edouard's going to codify it all into something the coach will actually accept."

Edouard didn't argue with the word, because it was true. He had spent the whole week torn between two ideas he couldn't yet reconcile: the old coach at his old club, who preached stillness, long holds, patience with the body, and the sprinters he watched online who seemed to be in constant motion before races, swinging legs, skipping, never once sitting into a stretch. Both looked certain. Both couldn't be right at the same moment, or maybe they could, and that possibility annoyed him more than choosing would have.

"Show me what you did before the time trial," he said to Dawson.

Dawson shrugged. "Held my hamstring stretch on the line. Proper one, a minute at least. Felt really loose." He paused, working the plum stone around his mouth. "Felt flat, though. Legs like they belonged to someone slower."

Edouard wrote that down, then looked at it. Samson leaned over his shoulder. "You think the stretching did that?"

"I think a long static hold, like sixty seconds or more on one muscle, right before something explosive, can knock your strength and power down for a bit," Edouard said. "So the fast guys warm up with dynamic movement instead. Leg swings, skips, stuff that moves."

"So you'd never stretch again?"

"I didn't say that." And he hadn't, and the distinction mattered to him more than he could explain. The stillness his old coach taught still felt true for other hours, other days, the long easy ones. It was the timing that had been wrong, the stacking of one truth directly on top of another where they didn't fit.

Samson had gone quiet, which was unusual, and Edouard noticed him flexing his left knee the way he did when it ached after hard sessions. "How's it feel today?" Edouard asked.

"Sore. It's fine."

"It's not fine if it's sore on Monday and you've written hills." Edouard pulled the pencil from behind his ear and drew a line through Tuesday in Samson's plan, then wrote rest in the space. "You can swim or bike easy if you go crazy sitting still. Knee first."

Samson looked at the page for a long moment. "Coach never asks about the knee."

"I know." Edouard kept his eyes on the grid he was building, because he understood that some things are easier to accept when nobody watches your face. In the margin he began listing warm-ups for each hard day: dynamic movements, done in order, timed against the session start so nothing long and static sat close to the gun. On the rest days he allowed the old coach's stillness, long unhurried holds, moved far from anything requiring power.

The sky had gone the color of a bruise turning better, and Dawson checked his phone. "I have to be home by seven."

"Ten minutes," Edouard said. He worked fast, the plan taking a shape he could almost defend: hard Monday, easy Tuesday, hard Wednesday, rest Thursday, hard Friday, short and sharp Saturday, full rest Sunday, with the knee rule written in for Samson and a note at the bottom saying the whole thing was provisional, that he'd change it if the results argued with it. Dawson crouched to reread it, and Edouard watched his lips move through the warm-up column.

"You're sure about the stretch thing?" Dawson asked.

"It's what the evidence says. Whether it's the whole truth for you, I don't know yet." Edouard turned the notebook around so Samson could see. "Neither of you has to trust my veracity. Monday, try it. Warm up moving, hold nothing long, and see what your legs tell you at the hundred mark."

Samson stood, brushed grass from his jeans, and folded his borrowed page into his pocket like something he intended to keep. "If I run faster," he said, "I'm calling it the Edouard plan."

"If you run faster, call it whatever you want and ice your knee."

Dawson laughed and laced his cleats against the fence, and Edouard sat back down alone at the picnic table, moving one stone aside, and in the last of the light added one more line under Saturday: leg swings, ten each side, then hand the stopwatch to whoever shows up.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: NOT EXISTS is another way to find customers with no orders: it keeps each customer for whom a subquery finds no matching order row.
story:
Kaitlyn sat cross-legged on the living room carpet with her laptop open on the coffee table, the screen tilted so the glare from the window wouldn't drown it out. Her mother's curtains, some diaphanous gray thing that had once been white, did almost nothing to block the afternoon light, so Kaitlyn had dragged the table two feet to the left, knocking over a stack of unopened mail in the process. On the screen were two database queries, both of which were supposed to answer the same question: which customers had never ordered anything.

The first query she had copied from a forum, a LEFT JOIN followed by a check for empty order rows. It worked. It returned six customers, and Tina, who was sprawled across the couch with her own laptop balanced on her knees, had already run it and gotten the same six. The second query was shorter and stranger, and Kaitlyn had written it herself from a paragraph she'd read at one in the morning.

"You're just staring at it," Tina said without looking up. "It's not a painting."

"It kind of is." Kaitlyn turned the laptop toward her. "Look. This one goes through every customer and, for each one, runs a little search inside the orders table. If the search comes up empty, it keeps the customer."

Tina leaned over, chewing the end of a pen she was not otherwise using. "So it keeps the people with nothing."

"Right. NOT EXISTS," Kaitlyn said, tapping the keyword. "It keeps each customer for whom the subquery finds no matching order row."

"Okay, but the first one already does that. Why learn two ways to be wrong?"

Kaitlyn had asked herself the same thing at one in the morning, and she had an answer she didn't entirely trust. The two queries agreed on the answer, but they disagreed about everything else, about what the question meant, about whether absence was something you joined to or something you checked for. She had been thinking about that distinction since Tuesday, when Mr. Navarro, who taught the computer science class and lived three doors down, had read her forum query aloud in a voice of theatrical sorrow.

"Who taught you this?" he had said, holding up her printed page. "A stranger on the internet, with a grudge?"

"It works," Kaitlyn had said.

"Lots of terrible things work. That's not the adage, but it should be." Then he had handed the page back and told her nothing else, which was his way of assigning homework that he'd deny assigning.

In the living room, Tina ran both queries again, side by side. Six names, then six names, identical. "Twins," Tina said. "Conjoined twins where one is really smug about being short."

"Mr. Navarro would excoriate me if I turned in the forum one. He'd do that thing where he doesn't yell, he just reads your code out loud slowly, like a eulogy." Kaitlyn pulled the laptop back and deleted the forum query entirely, then retyped it from memory, because she wanted to know whether she understood it or had only ever borrowed it. Her fingers knew where the joins went. That surprised her a little. She had spent most of the semester convinced she was the kind of person who copied things, a conviction based mainly on one group project in ninth grade where she had, in fairness, copied things.

The memory still had teeth. Christina, who had been in that group, had spent a week not speaking to her over it, and then spoken to her again as if nothing had happened, which in some ways was worse. Kaitlyn had never decided whether Christina's silence had been proportionate or just easy, whether being quietly angry was a form of forgiveness or just its costume. She thought about it now because the two queries on her screen kept insisting on their own version of the question: two true things, differently built, and no rule anywhere saying which one you were supposed to be.

Then Tina squinted at her screen and sat up so fast the laptop slid. "Wait. Rerun yours. I got seven."

"That's not possible, they were the same."

"They were the same five minutes ago. Rerun it."

Kaitlyn reran hers. Seven names. The sixth row of Tina's result was still there, but a new one had appeared at the bottom for Kaitlyn only: Christina Reyes, customer ID 114, no orders. Tina's query, the forum one, did not return her.

They both looked at the name for a while. Outside, a car door slammed; in the kitchen, the kettle started its low complaint. Kaitlyn scrolled to the test data Tina had loaded that morning, the sample rows Tina had typed in herself while Kaitlyn was retyping her query, and there it was: a customer row for Christina with an order row beside it, an order with a quantity of zero and a null product. Not no order. An order that was nothing.

"So which query is right?" Tina asked.

"Mine's answering the question we asked. Yours is answering a different question that sounds like ours." Kaitlyn stopped, because she could hear Mr. Navarro's voice in her own and wasn't sure she'd earned it yet. "Or mine's answering the question we should have asked. Depends on whether an empty order counts as nothing."

"That's very deep for a Saturday."

"That's a yes or no in the data, actually. We just haven't decided which."

Tina picked up her pen, held it like a gavel, and brought it down on the arm of the couch. "Decision: an empty order counts as nothing. Remove the row, rerun both, six and six, we go get food."

Kaitlyn deleted the null order, ran both queries, and watched the two identical lists bloom on the screen, Christina gone from hers, order restored to the world in every sense. Then she closed the laptop, put it under the mail she'd knocked over, and reached for her shoes.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Negative space is the empty area around and between the subjects of an image, and artists often draw that space to get a shape's outline right.
story:
The chair by the window on the second floor of the public library had a shape Ashton could not get right. He had drawn it four times in his sketchbook, and four times the legs came out like noodles, the seat like a trapezoid collapsing under its own ambition. The assignment from his art elective was due Friday: draw an ordinary object so that someone looking at it would know exactly which object it was, in all its particular stubbornness. He had chosen this chair because it was always empty and because nobody else would think a library chair was worth anything.

Khushi dropped into the seat across from him and slid a manga volume out of her backpack without taking off her headphones. Adem arrived a minute later with two granola bars and immediately began reading over Ashton's shoulder, which Ashton hated and tolerated in roughly equal measure.

"It looks like the chair is melting," Adem said, unwrapping a bar.

"Thank you. I hadn't noticed." Ashton turned the page and started again. The chair sat there, quiescent in the afternoon light, its wooden legs plain and refuseful of his pencil. The proportions were the problem. Every time he watched the legs, his hand invented curves that were not there.

Khushi pushed one headphone off her ear. "Why are you staring at the chair like it insulted you?"

"Because it did." He tapped the sketchbook. "I keep drawing what I think a chair is instead of this chair."

She leaned over, studied his page, then the actual chair, and made a small sound of recognition. "In that drawing book my mom got me, they called it negative space," she said. "You draw the empty parts around and between the subject instead of the subject. Like the gaps between the legs."

Ashton stared at her. "That sounds made up."

"Look it up if you want." She put her headphone back on, which was her way of saying she had contributed all she intended to contribute.

But the idea sat in him like a stone in a shoe. He looked again at the chair, this time at everything that was not the chair: the triangle of window between the stretchers, the wedge of carpet visible through the gap under the seat, the rectangles of light that the legs chopped out of the wall. He turned to a fresh page and drew those instead. He drew the shapes of nothing. And when the emptiness was down on the paper, the legs appeared around it, correct without his having drawn them, standing where they actually stood. He sat back, slightly betrayed by how easy it had been.

Adem leaned in. "Wait. You drew the gaps and the chair just showed up?"

"Apparently that's a thing. Artists do it to get the outline right." Ashton said it aloud half to convince himself, because it felt like a trick rather than a method, like the drawing had happened to him rather than through him. He thought of his father, who fixed engines by listening for what was missing, and of Ms. Park's lecture in history about mapping an empire's silences. He had always assumed you understood a thing by staring straight at it. Now he wondered whether he had drawn his whole life that way, outline first, and whether the outlines had been wrong.

Ms. Park appeared at the end of the shelf with a cart of returns, stopped, and looked at his open page for a long moment. "That's the window seat chair," she said. "People sit there for forty years and never once draw it." She ran a finger near the edge of the page without touching it. "The provenance of that chair, if anyone asks, is the 1988 renovation. It's the only survivor from the old reading room." Then she rolled the cart onward, leaving the fact behind her like something she had set down gently on the table.

Ashton copied the date in the corner of the page, then wondered whether he was allowed to wonder if that was true. It could portend nothing at all, an old woman's fond embellishment, or it could be the realest thing in the drawing, a chair that had outlived its whole room. He looked at the second sketch, the honest one, where the truth had come from the empties. He looked at the four failed chairs before it. Somewhere between staring at a thing and staring at its gaps, he thought, was where the thing actually lived, but he could not yet say how you stayed there, or whether you could stay there on purpose.

Adem crumpled the granola wrapper. "So are you turning in the gap one or the chair one?"

Ashton set the pencil down across both pages, right through the middle of the window's light, and did not answer yet.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Computing a binary search's midpoint as (low + high) / 2 can overflow on very large arrays; writing low + (high - low) / 2 gives the same middle without the overflow.
story:
The code printed PASS forty-one times before the bell for fourth period, and Alexia sat back in the computer lab with the particular satisfaction of a program that worked. Mr. Gupta had assigned the sorting-and-searching unit two weeks ago, and she had volunteered for the demonstration slot at the programming club's open evening, mostly because Lukas had said, in front of everyone, that she explained things better than she gave herself credit for. She was less sure of that than he was. What she knew was this: linear search starts at the first element and checks every one until it finds the target, while binary search works only on sorted data and halves the remaining range each time by checking the middle. She had said as much to her mother over dinner, using the phone book analogy, and her mother had nodded the way people nod at weather.

The club had also entered the regional team contest, and their solution to Problem C depended on a binary search over an array the judges had promised would be enormous. Lukas wanted the trophy for the school's display case, badly, because his older brother had won it twice and had a habit of burnishing those memories at family dinners until they shone more than they deserved. Kaden, who was newer to the team, mostly wanted not to be the reason they failed. Alexia wanted the open evening to go well, and she had promised to rehearse her explanation with Lukas after school, in the lab, with Mr. Gupta grading submissions at the front desk.

"Run it on the sample first," Lukas said, dropping into the chair beside her. He had his own laptop open to the contest's practice site, where the sample dataset for Problem C was posted: ten thousand entries. Alexia compiled, ran, and the terminal spat out the correct answer in under a second. Kaden leaned over her shoulder and exhaled, relieved, as though he had personally lifted something heavy.

"Okay, explanation," Lukas said. "Go. I'm a confused parent."

"Sorted data," Alexia began. "If it's sorted, you don't check items one by one. You look at the middle. If the middle is bigger than what you want, the answer, if it's there, is in the lower half, so you throw away the upper half. Then you take the middle of what's left, and so on. Each step cuts the search space in half." She turned the screen toward him. "On a million items, that's around twenty checks instead of a million."

"Instead of a million in the worst case," Kaden said, quietly. He had read the textbook more carefully than any of them.

"In the worst case," Alexia conceded, and Lukas wrote worst case on his palm with a pen, which she chose to interpret as commitment.

They submitted to the practice judge next, and the practice judge offered something the samples had not: a stress test, an array of the maximum size the contest allowed. Alexia uploaded their solution, and the judge returned a single line: RUNTIME ERROR. Not a wrong answer, which would have meant her logic was off, but a crash, which made no sense, because the program had just run perfectly.

"It works on the test data," Kaden said, as if saying it twice would make it true the second time.

Lukas pulled the keyboard toward himself and scrolled through her function, and the room got very quiet except for Mr. Gupta's pen at the front. "Here," Lukas said, tapping the screen. He pointed at the line where she computed the midpoint, the line that read mid = (low + high) / 2. "It's this." He looked at her, not smug, almost apologetic. "On a huge array it overflows. Low plus high gets too big."

Alexia stared at the line. She had written it in the first ten minutes of the assignment and never looked at it again, because it was the kind of line that seemed beyond suspicion, arithmetic so basic it couldn't be wrong. "Then what do you write instead?"

"You write low + (high - low) / 2," Lukas said. "Same middle. No overflow." He said it flatly, the way you read a fact off a card, and she copied it into the editor character by character, feeling the strange vertigo of a thing that fixed itself the moment it was named. She rebuilt, resubmitted, and the judge returned ACCEPTED, the word sitting in the terminal in unremarkable gray.

She sat with it for a moment. Her version and his version produced the same midpoint on every input she could test by hand; the difference only existed where the numbers got too large, in territory she had never visited and could not see. She thought of biology, of the genotype hidden inside an organism, the instructions there all along, invisible until something in the environment made them matter. The bug had been in her program like that, present from the first line, silent until the huge array called it out. She did not say any of this aloud, because it was half-formed, and because Lukas was already reopening the club's slide deck.

"You'll tell them this at the open evening," he said. "The parents like a disaster story."

"It wasn't a disaster."

"It'll be better than the trophy speech I'm writing, which is currently one scathing paragraph about the judges from last year." He grinned, and Kaden laughed, and Mr. Gupta looked up from his grading with the expression of a man deciding whether to intervene and, as usual, deciding not to.

At the open evening on Thursday, Alexia stood at the front of the lab with the projector behind her and twelve parents in folding chairs. She explained linear search first, walking a row of attendees and looking at each face, and then binary search, halving the room, halving it again.
