When she got to the bug, she put the two lines of code side by side on the slide, the one that crashed on huge arrays and the one that didn't, and admitted she still couldn't fully picture the moment where one of them broke. A woman in the second row raised her hand and asked which one she should teach her son.

"The one on the right," Alexia said, and pointed at the screen.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues' 1993 study of violinists described 'deliberate practice': effortful work on specific weaknesses with immediate feedback, not just logging hours.
story:
The eleven-year-olds called it the diamond, though the game they played had nothing to do with baseball, and the chalk lines had faded into the outfield grass where Naomi now set down a bag of cones. She had agreed to coach this team in March because Ms. Leung, who ran the neighborhood league out of the recreation center, had said the alternative was folding it. There was no money for a real coach; the league operated on donations and the borrowed field, indigent in a way that only became obvious when you saw the duct tape on the goal frames. So every Tuesday and Thursday since spring, Naomi had run scrimmages, because scrimmages were easy, because the kids loved them, and because for six weeks she had told herself that playing the game was the same as learning it.

The team passed the way young teams pass, which was to say barely at all. In a scrimmage a ball-carrier under pressure would freeze, then fling the ball in the general direction of a teammate, often into the flat grass where nobody stood. Six weeks of games and the pattern had not changed, and Naomi had begun to wonder about her own part in that. She kept a small notebook now, mostly to adjudicate between her competing instincts: the instinct to let them play and be happy, and the suspicion that she was supervising repetition rather than teaching anything at all.

Laetitia came to watch sometimes, sprawled on the bleachers with a binder of summer homework. That Thursday she was reading a printed article and kept looking up at the field with an expression Naomi knew meant she was about to be insufferable. "Ericsson," Laetitia said, when practice paused for water. "K. Anders Ericsson and some colleagues, 1993, a study of violinists. It's in my psych packet."

"I don't teach violin."

"You don't teach anything, that's the point." Laetitia waved the pages. "The violinists at the top hadn't just logged hours. The difference was what they called deliberate practice. Effortful work on specific weaknesses with feedback, right away. Your kids scrimmage for an hour and never hear a single thing about what they did wrong until the ball's already turned over and forgotten."

Naomi wanted to argue, and part of the argument was real: the kids were eleven, it was summer, nobody had paid for this. But the other part was just defensiveness, and she knew that too, the way you can hold a position and see through it simultaneously. She thought about a violinist in a small room repeating one difficult passage, hearing each mistake as it happened, correcting it before it hardened into habit. Then she thought about Maya dropping her stick to the grass every time she caught a pass, forty times a practice, unnoticed.

So she tried it. She cut the scrimmage to twenty minutes at the end and spent the first forty on one weakness she had circled in her notebook: passing under pressure. She paired them off, put a defender on each ball-carrier, and made the passer call the receiver's name before releasing, every single time. When a pass went wild, she stopped the pair right there and made them repeat it, and she stood behind Maya specifically, saying "hands up" the instant the stick began to droop. It was harder to watch than the scrimmages had been. The kids got frustrated; one boy sat down in the grass and had to be coaxed up by Oliver, who had started showing up to help and was better than Naomi at the coaxing. The feedback had to be immediate or it was nothing, she was learning that fast. Praise at the end of practice was too late, a letter mailed after the recipient had moved.

What she could not settle was the question of how much of the change to claim. Two weeks in, the passes in the Thursday scrimmage were crisper, more of them arriving, and Maya's hands came up without being told. Ms. Leung watched from the bleachers for a while and said, "Whatever you're doing, keep doing it," and Naomi said she would. But causality was a slippery thing to pin on a summer field. Maybe they were simply growing, or responding to Oliver's steadiness, or passing better because the novelty of any drill wears into competence. The violinists in the study had been measured against each other in a conservatory; Naomi had eleven kids on a chalk-faded diamond and no control group, no way to know what they would have become without her cones and her clipboard.

She wrote that uncertainty in her notebook, plainly, under the drill diagrams: can't prove it was the method. Then, because Thursday had gone well and the light was going amber over the outfield, she let the scrimmage run ten minutes long. Maya took a pass under pressure, hands high, and whipped the ball cross-field to a girl who caught it clean and shot wide, and every kid on the grass screamed with delight anyway.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: One of Amazon's leadership principles, 'Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit', asks employees to respectfully challenge a decision they disagree with, then commit fully once it is made.
story:
The red pen came back on Thursday, and Mason counted the marks twice before he said anything to anyone. Seventeen points off the geology essay, and under the grade Mr. Wilson had written a single line: tone drifts informal in paragraphs four and five; see rubric. The essay had been about sedimentary rock, about how the Grand Canyon's layered walls kept a record nobody had intended to keep, and Mason thought paragraphs four and five were the best ones. He thought they were the honest ones.

At lunch he spread the pages across the table between Cheyenne's tray and Aurelia's backpack. "He wants me to sound like a lawyer," he said. "That's not writing, that's camouflage."

Aurelia pulled the pages closer and read for a while, chewing the inside of her cheek. "He's not saying your ideas are wrong. He's saying your words lean on him. Like here, where you call his rubric 'arbitrary.'"

"It is arbitrary."

"Then prove it instead of naming it." Cheyenne pointed at the margin with her fork. "You impugn the guy's whole system in one sentence and then act surprised when he takes points off. Write it like it matters to you, not like it's beneath you."

Mason gathered the pages. "So I'm supposed to just swallow it."

"Nobody said that," Aurelia said. But she didn't say what he was supposed to do either, and he carried the ambiguity home like a stone in his jacket pocket.

His mother was at the kitchen counter with her laptop open, eating cold noodles out of the container. She worked in an office Mason had never visited, doing something with shipping schedules, and most nights her job stayed at that distance. Tonight she was muttering at the screen, and when he asked, she waved him over. "My whole team wanted a different warehouse route. We argued it for a week. We lost."

"So now what?"

"Now we do it the way it was decided, and we do it hard." She closed the laptop halfway. "Where I work, it's one of Amazon's leadership principles. 'Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit.' You respectfully challenge a decision you disagree with, then commit fully once it's made." She shrugged, as if it were a small thing. "The backbone part is easy. The commit part is where people fall down."

Mason sat with that while she reheated the noodles, and then he went upstairs and opened his email. The blank message to Mr. Wilson sat there for a long time. He typed "this grade is unfair," deleted it, typed "with respect, I'd like to contest the deduction," and deleted that too, because it sounded like a lawyer, exactly the thing he'd complained about. What Aurelia had actually shown him was that the form wasn't the enemy of the feeling. The form was how the feeling got taken seriously.

The email he finally sent had a subject line, a greeting, and three short paragraphs. In the first, he named the assignment and the deduction. In the second, he laid out his reasoning in order: the rubric penalized informal tone, not weak argument, and paragraphs four and five contained his strongest evidence, the stratigraphic detail he'd spent a weekend verifying. He asked directly whether the deduction reflected the rubric or his style, and he asked it as a question, not an accusation. In the third, he wrote that if Mr. Wilson looked at it again and the grade still stood, Mason would accept the grade and revise the essay to the rubric without further argument.

Mr. Wilson's reply arrived the next morning, before first period. It was shorter than Mason expected. He thanked Mason for the message, noted that it was the clearest thing Mason had written all semester, and said that on rereading, paragraphs four and five were indeed the strongest, and the tone there was a feature, not a flaw. He adjusted the grade by eight points, not seventeen. "The remaining deduction," he wrote, "stands for the other sections. I'm offering revision amnesty until Friday for anyone who wants it, but you've earned the right to leave this one alone. Your choice."

Mason read the email three times, once in the hallway, once in chemistry, once on his phone under the desk. He didn't know yet which he'd choose, whether eight points was enough or whether he wanted the other nine badly enough to sand down sentences he liked. At lunch he showed Aurelia and Cheyenne the thread, and Cheyenne read it and slid the phone back.

"So you're going to commit either way," she said. "You already did. Look at your last paragraph."

Mason looked. He'd made a promise before he knew how it would end, and it had held.

That night he opened the essay, scrolled to paragraph four, the one about the canyon's walls holding their record in patient layers, and left it exactly as it was.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own, published in 1929, argues that a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction.
story:
Ms. Owusu had written two words on the board, "Marxist" and "feminist," and under them a page number from Jane Eyre, and Hunter had spent the first ten minutes of class pretending he already understood the difference between analyzing a book and accusing it. The passage was the one where Jane, small and plain and hired out as a governess, stands in a drawing room full of people who do not look at her. Their assignment was to say what the passage was quietly arguing, and Hunter wanted, more than he could admit, to get it right, because the last essay he had handed in had come back with a single comment in the margin: "Plot summary. Where are you?"

"Okay," Ms. Owusu said, tapping the board. "Groups of three. Find the passage's assumptions about money and about women, and tell me whether the book supports them or exposes them."

Amari dragged her desk over to his, and Shane followed, chewing the cap of a pen he had borrowed in September and never returned. They read the page again in silence. Jane notices the rug, the porcelain, the fire laid in a grate she will never own.

"So for the Marxist thing," Shane said, "she's basically an employee. Like the rug is there to remind her she isn't."

"That's not nothing," Amari said, "but you're skipping who she is. She's a woman being paid to be invisible. That's two arguments stacked on top of each other."

Hunter had the book open and was looking at the sentence about the fire. He remembered, suddenly and inconveniently, an afternoon in eighth grade when he had told a girl in his class that she only won the essay contest because the judges felt bad. He had never apologized. He had never even thought of it as an accusation that needed retracting until right now, sitting in a room where they were being asked to ask who got to write the books at all.

"Wait," he said. "The question isn't just what happens to Jane. It's who wrote this. Like, why is the reading list mostly men?"

Amari turned her pen over. "Actually, we did this last year. Virginia Woolf, A Room of One's Own, published in 1929. She argues a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction."

"That's the whole thing?" Shane said.

"That's the whole foundation of it," Amari said.

Hunter wrote it down, and under it he wrote "Jane Eyre, 1847," though he wasn't sure yet what the gap between those years meant, only that it meant something. He thought of Woolf's sentence as a kind of synecdoche, the one room standing for every material condition an artist needs and rarely gets, though he did not say that out loud because he was still testing whether it was true.

"So here's my read," he said slowly. "The Marxist lens says Jane is a worker in a rich house, and the rich house needs her poor. Fine. But the feminist lens asks a different question. It asks why the person noticing all this, Charlotte Brontë, was almost the only woman on a list of forty books. And Woolf's answer is money and a room. Not talent. Not permission. Money and a room."

"Which exonerates nobody," Amari said. "The men weren't better. They were funded."

"Or it's not that simple," Shane said, pointing at the page. "Brontë did write this. Without the room, supposedly. So is Woolf wrong?"

Ms. Owusu, drifting between desks, paused at their row. "Don't ask me. Argue it on paper."

Hunter looked at the sentence about the fire again. He had started the class thinking the assignment was about catching old books being wrong, convicting them from the safety of the present, and now it felt more like the passage was catching him, showing him a door he had walked past every day without registering it. Whether Brontë had beaten the odds or quietly disproved Woolf, he could not decide, and he noticed, with some surprise, that the indecision was not uncomfortable. It felt like the actual work.

He began to write. First the claim, then the counterclaim, then a line he underlined twice: the reading list is not a ranking of genius; it is a record of who could afford the paper. When the bell rang he kept writing, and Amari waited by the door, and Shane said, "You coming or not?"

"In a minute," Hunter said, and kept his pen moving.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Hokusai's print series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, made around 1830 to 1832, actually contains 46 prints, because ten were added after the first 36 sold well.
story:
Colton counted the canvases leaning against the kiln twice, and both times the number came to eleven. The art room smelled of turpentine and the vinegar tang of the etching bath, and outside the windows the parking lot was emptying car by car. The portfolio was supposed to be ten finished pieces around one theme, with an artist's statement, and he had eleven, and the eleventh was the one he liked best.

"Ten means ten," Mr. MacLeod said from the doorway. He was stacking stools, not looking over. "The rubric is not jurisprudence, Colton. There's no appeal court."

"Then I'll cut one."

"You'll decide which one is yours and which one is showing off." He set the last stool upside down on a table and left, keys jangling.

Colton sat on the floor between the canvases and pulled his sketchbook onto his knee. He had started the theme in September, when his grandfather's house was being emptied and his mother had let him take the kitchen window, an actual window, sash and all, because he said he wanted to paint what people leave behind. Nine of the paintings were rooms: the kitchen with the window propped in it, the shed, the stairwell with the bulb he remembered his grandfather replacing in October, though that was a memory, not evidence. The tenth was the house from the street at dusk. The eleventh was the kitchen again, painted after he'd gone back alone in November, when the wallpaper was already peeling where the humidity had gotten in.

Angela came in with her own portfolio under her arm, stopped, and looked at the row on the floor. "You have too many."

"I know."

"No, I mean it's a good problem." She sat down across from him, cross-legged, unwrapping a granola bar she didn't offer to share. "Did I tell you about Hokusai? I found it last night for my statement thing." She pointed at the painting of the wave print taped above the sink, the one Mr. MacLeod kept there like a poster of a saint. "That's from Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. It's a print series he made around 1830 to 1832, and it actually contains forty-six prints, because ten were added after the first thirty-six sold well." She took a bite. "It outgrew its own title. Nobody made him take the extra ten down."

"That's different. That's Hokusai."

"It's exactly not different, actually, but fine."

She got up to rinse her hands and he watched the water run over her fingers while she talked about her own theme, which was hands, all hands, her mother's hands and her own and the hands of the cashier at the pharmacy, and he thought about the word enthrall and how he had used it in his draft statement, that the emptied rooms enthralled him, and how Mr. MacLeod had written "too strong?" beside it in red pencil. He could hear the teacher's sardonic voice in the margin even now, could see him at his desk in September saying, "Enthralled, Colton? Or just unwilling to stop?"

He remembered then the day his grandfather had taken the kitchen window apart himself, three years ago, because the putty had failed. Colton had been fourteen and had sat on the counter handing him the scraper, and his grandfather had said the glass was older than the house, that it had come from somewhere else, a church or a school or nobody remembered. Colton had believed him completely and later understood that his grandfather made things up, that this was a way he loved people, giving them something to hold onto. The eleventh painting had that window in it, and the made-up story lived in it too, though nobody looking would know.

Leonie appeared in the doorway with her camera, photographing everyone's work for the yearbook spread, and she crouched and framed the row of canvases. "Which one's not going in?"

"Undecided."

"You should keep the second kitchen," she said, standing. "The light's better and the wallpaper's coming off like it's meant to."

After she left he laid the two kitchens side by side. The first was cleaner, more composed, the window centered like a formal portrait. The second was messier and truer, and it argued with the first, and that argument was the whole point of going back alone in November, though he hadn't let himself think it in those words until now. He remembered what Angela had said about the ten extra prints, added because the first ones sold, and he understood something small and crooked about it: the series had kept going because people wanted more, not because the artist had finished saying it. He could not tell which situation he was in.

He took out his phone and opened the draft statement, deleted "enthrall," typed it back, deleted it again. Then he pulled the street-at-dusk painting out of the row and carried it to the rack by the kiln, and stood there with his hand still on its edge, not letting go yet. Angela was still at the sink, drying her hands on a paper towel.

"Take the kitchen one to the rack," she said without turning around.

"I know which one I'm taking," he said, and did not move.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: In countries where tax is withheld from pay, such as the US and Canada, a tax refund means more was withheld during the year than was owed; it is an overpayment returned, not extra income.
story:
Megan spread the papers across the kitchen table: her first pay stub from the hardware store, a shoebox of receipts, and the tax return her father had printed for her because she was eighteen now and had to file. She had been at the job since September, eleven hours a week stocking shelves and running the till, and she still did not fully understand where her money went between the register and her bank account.

The stub was the first puzzle. Gross pay, $412. Then a column of smaller numbers beneath it, each with an abbreviation she had to squint at. Federal tax withheld, $41. Provincial tax, $9. CPP, $18. EI, $7. Net pay, $337. She copied the numbers into her notebook and looked at the difference, $75, money that had existed on paper and then did not arrive in her account. Nobody had asked her whether she wanted to give it. It had simply been withheld, the way a landlord withholds a deposit, and she was supposed to trust that somewhere there was an accounting.

Her phone buzzed on the table. It was Sami, messaging from the lineup at the bank: "got my refund deposited. 600 bucks of free money. I'm buying the boots." A photo followed, the deposit confirmation, the number glowing at the top of the screen. Megan typed back a question mark, and Sami answered with three party emojis, as though the government had simply handed him six hundred dollars out of generosity, like a lottery paid to everyone who filed.

Megan set the phone down and pulled the return toward her. Line by line it asked for what she had earned and what had been withheld, the same numbers from the stub, the $41 and the $9, added across four months of pay. Then it walked the arithmetic toward a total tax owed. She followed it twice, because the first time she assumed she had made an error. The amount owed was less than the amount withheld. The difference, $97, was printed on a line labelled refund.

She sat with that for a moment. It was not a gift. It was the overpayment coming back, the gap between what had been taken from her paycheques and what she actually owed, returned to her a year later without interest. She thought of Sami at the bank, exhilarated by the deposit, already spending it in his head, calling it free money when it had been his money all along, held the whole time. She picked up the phone and typed carefully, deleting and retyping twice, then sent: "It's not extra income. They took too much out of your pay and they're giving the overpayment back." Sami replied with a single "wait what" and then, a minute later, "so I gave the government an interest-free loan." She wrote back, "basically," and left it there, because the rest of the metaphysics, whether withholding was theft or thrift or just administration, was more than she could settle over text.

The receipts were the other half of the evening. She had kept them in the shoebox because a girl at work, Brogan, had said you should keep receipts, and Megan had not asked for what. Now she laid them out: bus passes, work boots, a coffee every shift, the calculator she had bought for night school. At the bottom of each one the totals did not match the stickers. $34.99 became $39.42. A second, smaller number sat under the first, labelled HST, and it was on everything, the boots and the coffee alike, a percentage that gathered invisibly onto each purchase the way the deductions had gathered onto her pay. She added the tax she had paid at the till to the tax that had come off her cheque and wrote the sum in her notebook. It was less than the price of the boots Sami was about to buy with his own returned money.

Her father came through the kitchen for water and paused at the table, the papers, the notebook, the shoebox. "You're doing the return yourself?" he asked.

"Mostly," Megan said. "Did you know a refund is just them giving back what they over-took?"

"Your mother used to call it found money every spring," he said, and shrugged, and carried his glass out of the room.

Megan looked at the $97 line one more time. She had wanted it to be a windfall and it had turned out to be a correction, and she could not decide whether that made the system fair or merely precise, whether it was better to be overcharged and repaid than to be trusted with the full amount in the first place. The return did not offer an opinion. It only asked its questions in order, and she answered the last of them, signed her name in blue ink, and folded the receipts back into the shoebox.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Johann Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815, drawing on a design by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel.
story:
Isabella found the metronome on top of the piano, which was strange, because she was almost certain it had never been there before. It was a small wooden pyramid, dark with age, with a brass pendulum and a sliding weight, and when she wound it, the whole room began to tick like a patient clock. Her mother came in from the kitchen, drying her hands on a towel, and said, "That was your grandfather's. It's been sitting there since before you were born." Isabella said, "I know that," which was not exactly true, and wound it again just to hear it.

She had been taking piano lessons for exactly three weeks, a decision made in a moment of late-August ambition that now required daily defense. Her teacher, Mr. Chukwu, who lived two streets over and taught from a studio smelling of coffee and old paper, had given her a single maxim on the first day: practice slowly, he said, so slowly that you cannot make a mistake. Isabella had nodded and then, in every session since, played too fast and made dozens.

That evening she texted Emmanuel, because Emmanuel knew everything about anything mechanical, in the way of a boy who took apart toasters for fun. "Do you know who invented the metronome?" she wrote. "Asking for me." He wrote back almost immediately, which meant he was avoiding his own homework: "Johann Maelzel patented it in 1815. But he drew on a design by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel, so there's a whole argument about who really deserves the credit. People were furious about it for years." She read it twice, then looked at the little pyramid ticking on the piano, its pendulum swinging like it owed somebody money.

"Winkel got robbed," she announced the next day at lunch, setting her tray down across from Ellis. "Maelzel patented the thing in 1815, but the actual design came from Winkel first. It's basically theft with paperwork."

Ellis looked at her over a carton of chocolate milk. "You've been playing piano for three weeks and you're already having historiographical disputes."

"I'm having a justice issue."

"You're procrastinating," Ellis said, which stung because it was fair. Isabella had a lesson that afternoon and had practiced, by her own generous count, four times this week, a count that included one session of roughly eleven minutes during which she mostly watched the metronome tick.

She would have ruminate over that accusation all through French class, and she did, turning it over like a stone in her pocket, except that Mr. Chukwu's lesson came first. He met her at the studio door and she confessed everything at once, the skipped practices, the eleven minutes, the fascination with the metronome instead of the music. She braced for disappointment. Instead he laughed, a short warm sound, and said, "Good. You're interested in something. Now let's aim it."

He set her hands on the keys and put the tempo at sixty, one tick per second, slow enough that the silence between notes became its own instrument. "Winkel versus Maelzel," he said, as she played. "Who do you side with?" She said Winkel, obviously, the designer deserved the credit, and Mr. Chukwu made a noncommittal noise that she suspected was deliberate. He had a habit of doing that, offering her two positions and refusing to pick, and she suspected he did it to be annoying, and also, on worse days, because he thought she should learn to hold an argument herself.

That night she did practice, genuinely, forty whole minutes, because she had a plan. The plan was this: she would slow the metronome down until the piece was perfect, then speed it up notch by notch, so that perfection would be smuggled upward inside speed. It did not work, or it worked only partly; at the slow tempo her fingers were flawless, and the moment she slid the weight up, her left hand deserted her like a fair-weather friend. She tried to tell herself the fault was in the machine, some inconsistency in the ticking, and even as she formed the thought she recognized it as specious, the kind of excuse that sounds reasonable only to the person making it. The metronome was not the problem. The metronome was never the problem.

Later she texted Ellis a full report: "Progress. Left hand unreliable. The metronome is blameless. Winkel remains robbed." Ellis replied with a single thumbs-up and the message "piano criminal," which she decided to accept as friendship.

The following week she brought the question back to Mr. Chukwu, because it kept bothering her, the way small injustices do. "I still think Maelzel was wrong," she said. "But." She paused, hands resting on keys she now knew well enough to be embarrassed in front of. "If he hadn't patented it, would anybody have Winkel's name at all? Nobody remembers the people who only invent things. They remember the people who put them on pianos." Mr. Chukwu considered this with the seriousness he gave to real questions, which always surprised her a little, and said only, "So who was more important?" She said that was a bad question, that credit and usefulness were different things, and that she was allowed to hold both opinions at once as long as she knew which one she was holding. He wrote something in his notebook, and she had a feeling, not entirely comfortable, that it was about her.

Her mother passed through the living room while Isabella practiced that evening, the metronome ticking at sixty, her hands finally, at last, landing where they were supposed to land. Her mother paused in the doorway, listening, and Isabella, without stopping, said, "Did you know Maelzel only patented it in 1815? The real design was Winkel's. Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel." Her mother said she had not known that, and Isabella slid the brass weight up a notch, and the little pyramid ticked faster.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: In 1896, Swedish scientist Svante Arrhenius made the first calculation of how much Earth would warm if the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubled.
story:
The permit said the site had to be cleared by noon, which gave Eric and his two classmates until Saturday evening to finish the presentation they had promised Mr. Sok on Monday. They had brought a laminated printout of the Keeling curve, a roll of graph paper, and Eric's crumpled notes from the planetarium talk in the spring, and now they sat around a cooler on which Maria was drawing the atmosphere in chalk.

"Start with sunlight," she said, tapping the cooler's lid. "Shortwave comes in, hits the ground, and the ground gives back longwave. That's the part I always forget." Oceane, who was turning a marshmallow over the coals with unnecessary patience, asked the question that had been circling all afternoon: whether it mattered that they could not demonstrate any of this, only describe it. "You can't show a classroom a molecule," she said. "You can only show them the graph."

Eric unrolled the printout and weighted its corners with stones. The line rose in small saw-toothed steps, climbing decade over decade, and he had learned in the last week to read it the way you read a heartbeat, the yearly wobble being the northern forests breathing in and out. He traced the slope with one finger and thought about how his grandfather, who drove trucks for forty years, called all of it a scam at Thanksgiving. Eric had not argued. He had gone home and looked things up instead, and what he found did not feel like ammunition; it felt like a landscape he was only beginning to walk into. Was certainty something you owed people, or was honest doubt its own kind of respect?

"The saw teeth," Maria said, leaning over his shoulder. "Explain them to me again, but as if I'm your grandfather." Eric tried. He said the forests inhale in summer, and she nodded, and Oceane, never one to let a good thing pass, said, "Now do it as if I'm a facetious college freshman who thinks every graph is fake." Eric laughed and gave the freshman a hundred years of measurements taken on a volcano in Hawaii, and the freshman, having no answer, ate her marshmallow.

The trouble came at the part Eric had been dreading. In the notes from the planetarium talk, a student had asked whether climate predictions only started with computers, whether all of it was too new to trust. A friend beside him had looked it up on her phone and read the answer aloud, and Eric had copied it in pencil and now could not read his own handwriting. He remembered the shape of it: someone, surprisingly early, had worked out a number for warming. "Swedish," Maria guessed. "Everything old in physics is Swedish." Oceane said that guessing was pointless and held her phone toward the sky, hunting for one bar of signal on the ridge above the campsite. They had until dark to settle the slide, because the drive home was Sunday and Monday morning belonged to Mr. Sok.

Oceane came back down the ridge holding the phone above her head like a lantern. "In 1896," she read, "Swedish scientist Svante Arrhenius made the first calculation of how much Earth would warm if the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubled." She said it twice so Eric could type it. He sat with the sentence for a moment. A man with paper and a pencil, before cars filled the roads, before the curve on his graph had begun its climb, had already asked the question Eric was preparing to ask a classroom on Monday. There was something in that which problematized his grandfather's argument and also, strangely, Eric's own. If the question was that old, then the doubt was newer than the science, not the other way around, and he had never thought of it in that order before.

"So do we lead with him or with the graph?" Maria asked. It was nearly dark and the slide had to be finished before the lantern died. Eric looked from the printout, with its patient rising line, to his grandfather in his mind, sitting at the head of a table. Maybe you could hold both at once, the way you hold a genus of things that look different but share a structure: the man with the pencil in 1896, the kids at the cooler now, the man who drove trucks and loved his grandchildren. Maybe the presentation could say plainly what was measured and how, and also say what nobody could yet say for certain, and let the room sit with that.

He wrote Arrhenius into the slide, then underneath it a question he did not have an answer for: what would you want to be true before you believed a thing? Oceane read it over his shoulder and said, "Mr. Sok is going to eat that alive." "Good," Eric said, and clicked off the lantern.

In the morning they packed the tent in the dark to make the noon deadline, and Maria scraped the chalk atmosphere off the cooler with the edge of a spork. Oceane folded the graph printout along its old creases and handed it to Eric, since Monday was his to carry. "Read me the line one more time," she said, and he did, from memory, all the way to doubled, while the car idled at the gate and the ranger waited to lock it behind them.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: A Marxist reading often asks whose labour makes the characters' comfortable lives possible, noticing servants and workers the novel mentions only in passing.
story:
Grace had claimed the reading nook by the window before dinner, her mother's old cushions stacked behind her back and a paperback of the novel open on her knees. The assignment sheet lay flattened on the armrest, and at the top of it, circled twice, was the deadline: tomorrow, first period, Mr. Nkosi, one page on a critical lens of her choosing. She had picked Marxism mostly because Kadence had picked feminism and it had seemed lazy to hand in matching essays. Now, with the night closing in, she was no longer sure what the lens was actually for.

She read the chapter again with a pencil in her hand, this time doing what Mr. Nkosi had suggested offhandedly at the end of class: read for who is in the room, not just who is talking. The drawing room filled with people, the picnic arranged, the carriage ordered. Somewhere in the middle of it she noticed a footman carrying a tray, and she thought, oddly, that she had read past him three times tonight without once seeing him.

"Wait," she said out loud to the empty nook. She took a fresh sheet of paper and drew two columns. In the left one she started counting every time the chapter mentioned a servant, cook, footman, gardener, maid, named or not. In the right one she counted how many times any of them actually spoke. The pencil moved down the page. Mentions climbed past a dozen. The speech column held one entry, a maid announcing that the carriage was ready, four words, and then nothing else for the rest of the chapter. She looked at the lopsided columns for a long moment, feeling something shift under her, the way a staircase feels wrong when you expected one more step.

She texted Kadence, who was doing the feminist lens on the same chapter. "Are you counting anything or just vibes." The reply came while Grace was still chewing her pencil: "counting how many times the women get interrupted lol. why." Grace typed: "I counted the servants. They're everywhere and they never talk. Like the whole picnic just appears." She sat with the phone in her lap, watching the typing bubble appear and disappear, and then Kadence wrote, "huh. whose labour makes the picnic happen though? that's not the women either." Grace read that twice. She had been so trained to follow the people the novel loved that she had never once asked the question Kadence had just asked by accident.

The problem was that Grace had been planning to write about the engagement plot, about whether the heroine's marriage choice was really a choice. That essay had a shape already; she knew where it ended. This other thing had no shape. It was more like a crack. She tried to explain it to herself in the margin: the beautiful manners of the drawing room were a kind of veneer, a polished surface, and underneath it somebody had polished the silver, carried the coal, cooked the meal, all without the novel thinking it worth recording. The dour footman with the tray had more to do with the heroine's afternoon than the heroine would ever admit, and the book itself would not admit it either.

She tried the lenses against each other, the way you press two maps together to see if the roads line up. The feminist reading asked who gets to choose. The Marxist reading, she wrote slowly, testing it, asks whose labour makes the comfortable lives possible, whose work has to be invisible for the picnic to feel effortless. They were not the same question, but they were not enemies either. The maid announcing the carriage was a woman doing labour nobody counted twice. Grace underlined that and then sat back, uneasy, because it felt true and also felt like a neat bow she was tying before she had earned it. What about the footman? What did he want? The novel would never say, and her essay could not invent it, and that hole was starting to feel like the most honest thing on the page.

Her mother called something about tea from the kitchen, and Grace carried the book and the counting sheet to the counter and read the numbers aloud while her mother sliced bread. "Fourteen mentions," she said. "One line of speech, four words." Her mother looked at the lopsided columns and said that sounded like most of her own days, and laughed, and Grace laughed too, but she wrote the exchange down afterward because it belonged to the essay somehow, a count taken at a kitchen counter.

Back in the nook, with an hour left before she made herself sleep, Grace began the page for Mr. Nkosi. She wrote the two columns into it, and the question about invisible labour, and then she wrote the thing she could not resolve: that both lenses together could open the book, and neither could tell her what the silent footman thought about any of it. She left that in, ragged edge and all. Outside the window the streetlight came on, and somewhere down the block a delivery van idled, its engine running so that somebody's groceries could arrive warm. Grace watched it until it pulled away.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: A 2011 analysis of the Dunedin Study found that children with lower self-control were more likely to have poorer health, less wealth and criminal convictions as adults.
story:
Jaxon sat in the waiting area outside the guidance office with a permission slip in his hand, watching the door with Ms. Dlamini's name on it in gold letters that had worn to brass at the edges. He had been sent here for skipping his Tuesday shift at the after-school program twice in one month, and the slip said "attendance concern," which was a phrase that made a small thing sound like a court document.

"Hey," said Eugene, sliding into the chair beside him, still in his gym clothes. "She call you in too?"

"She called me in. Nobody called you anywhere, you just followed me."

"I'm keeping you company. Moral support." Eugene leaned over to read the slip. "You skipped twice. That's it? Moses skips constantly."

"Moses got a warning already. I heard Ms. Dlamini kept him after class on Thursday." Jaxon folded the slip into quarters and then into eighths, until it was a small dense square that fit inside his fist. He had skipped because the shifts were boring, because the kids he supervised wanted to play dodgeball and he wanted to lie in the park with his phone, and because the two things felt entirely separate, like boxes in different rooms of a large house. He had a talent for that kind of arrangement. He could compartmentalize the job from the transcript, the transcript from college, college from whatever came after college, and never once notice the doors between the rooms.

The office door opened and a senior came out looking relieved, and Ms. Dlamini stood in the doorway in her grey cardigan and said, "Jaxon, come in," and Eugene mouthed good luck as the door closed behind them.

The office was small and smelled of the fern on the windowsill. On the wall behind her desk was a poster about future planning, and on the desk itself, next to the attendance file, lay a printed article with a paragraph highlighted in yellow. She turned it face down before he sat, but not before he read the top of the page: it said Dunedin Study, and below that, 2011.

"So," she said. "Two shifts."

"Two shifts," he agreed. "It won't happen again."

"I hear that from a lot of people, and most of them mean it." She opened his file, but she was watching him rather than the page. "What I can't figure out is whether you understand what the shifts are for. Do you?"

He started to say yes and then found he had stopped, because the honest answer was that he had never thought about it. The shifts were for money, forty dollars a week, and for the line on his applications that said community involvement. The kids were for supervising. Beyond that the thing had no inside to it, just a surface he touched twice a week.

"What's the article?" he asked.

She hesitated, then turned it over, and he read the highlighted paragraph standing up, leaning over her desk. It said that in 2011 an analysis of the Dunedin Study, which had followed a thousand people from birth in one New Zealand town, had found that children with lower self-control were more likely to have poorer health, less wealth and criminal convictions as adults. He read it twice. "Self-control," he said slowly. "Like, not skipping shifts."

"Like not skipping shifts," she said. "Among other things. But I didn't bring you here to lecture you, and I'm not going to explain that to you, because you just read it yourself." She took the paper back and set it under the file. "What I want to know is what you think it means. You're sixteen. Everything feels far away to you. Health, wealth, all of it. But the study followed kids who were exactly your age once."

He sat back down. The fern's shadow moved on the wall, and somewhere down the hall a locker slammed twice, and he thought about Moses, who skipped constantly and laughed about it, whose laughing made skipping seem like freedom rather than subtraction. And he thought about his own father, who had wanted to be an engineer and instead worked at the plant, and who said, on the subject of his own youth, only ever, "I did what I did," which was a sentence Jaxon had always found both moving and useless, a kind of erudition turned backward, all that knowledge arriving too late to change anything.

"Here's my problem with it," he said finally. "Those kids in the study, they didn't know they were being studied. Every choice they made, they made it as if it were small. Skipping one thing. That's not malevolent, that's just Tuesday. And then it turns out Tuesday was the whole thing."

"That's a good problem to have with it," Ms. Dlamini said.

"But it could also be wrong. Maybe the kids with low self-control had other stuff going on, stuff nobody wrote down." He turned the folded slip over in his fingers. "I don't know. It's one study. But even if it's only partly true, I can't check later. There's no draft of this."

"There isn't," she said.

He stood up, and she signed the slip, and he took it back to the hallway where Eugene was waiting, and Eugene asked him what happened in there, what did she say, and Jaxon looked down the corridor toward the gym where Moses was probably already gone for the day.

"Tuesday," Jaxon said, and started walking back toward the after-school room.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The electron transport chain sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane, where oxygen is the final electron acceptor and combines with protons to form water.
story:
The biology field trip had been pitched to Emma's class as a visit to the new cellular biology wing, which turned out to be one long dark corridor of glowing models, and by eleven o'clock she had learned exactly one thing for certain: the gift shop sold a plush mitochondrion with a label calling it "the powerhouse of the cell," which Priscilla had declared tautological, since the label might as well have read "this toy is the thing this toy is."

"Say that again slower," Emma said.

"I'm saying the label tells you nothing. It's like naming a lion the king of the savanna and expecting you to now understand lions." Priscilla squeezed the plush toy's middle. Josie was already three exhibits ahead, waving them toward a wall of light.

The wall was the reason they had come. Mr. Tehrani, their teacher, had promised that anyone who could walk the whole interactive display, glucose to ATP, without a wrong answer would get extra credit, and Emma needed the extra credit the way a drowning person needs a rope. Her last test had featured a question about oxygen's role in respiration, and she had written a paragraph of confident nonsense that Mr. Tehrani had returned with a single red circle around the word "breathing." She had not yet forgiven herself, or him.

The exhibit worked like a video game. You touched a molecule of glucose on the screen and dragged it through the steps, and if you made a mistake the screen went amber and an apologetic voice said try again. Emma's glucose broke apart cleanly. Pyruvate, check. The krebs cycle was a conveyor belt of little spinning shapes, and she sorted them with Josie hissing encouragement over her shoulder. Then the screen showed a cross-section of a mitochondrion, folded and gleaming, and asked: where does the electron transport chain sit?

"Outer membrane," Emma said, and touched it.

The screen went amber.

"Inner," Josie said. "It's the inner mitochondrial membrane. Look at the picture, it's all folded in there like curtains."

Emma touched the folded membrane and the screen bloomed green, and a stream of little electrons began to hop along a chain of protein shapes embedded in it, like stones across a stream. At the end of the chain there was a gap. The screen asked: what accepts the electron at the very end?

Here was where her test answer lived, the paragraph of nonsense. She had written that oxygen was breathed in to energize the blood, or something equally ceremonial, and she stood in front of the screen feeling the old sentence sit in her like a splinter.

"Priscilla," she called. "What do you know about oxygen?"

"Nothing," Priscilla said cheerfully. "I know it's in the air and I'm fond of it."

Emma touched the oxygen symbol anyway, on a hunch she could not have defended, and the screen accepted it. A small blue molecule of oxygen appeared at the end of the chain and took the electron, and then took protons too, drifting in from elsewhere, and the little animation joined them together into water. Ordinary water, H2O, the stuff in her water bottle, forming inside the folds of a mitochondrion inside a cell inside her.

"Wait," Emma said out loud. "Wait, wait. The oxygen I breathe in, it ends up as water? Inside me?"

"Apparently," Josie said, leaning in. "Every breath. You're a waterfall factory."

"That can't be right." Emma backed up the animation and ran it again, and again the oxygen sat at the end of the chain, the final acceptor, taking the last electron and then the protons, and becoming water. She ran it a third time. She thought about how she had been predicating her whole understanding on the idea that oxygen was a kind of fuel, something burned, something consumed like gasoline, and how the display was telling her something stranger: that oxygen was a destination. The electrons fell toward it like water finding the sea.

Mr. Tehrani drifted past with his clipboard. "How's it going?"

"Is this real?" Emma asked, pointing at the little blue water molecule. "Or is it a cartoon simplification?"

"It's the standard account," he said, and moved on toward a group arguing near the exit, because he was contractually forbidden, per his own field trip rules, from lecturing.

Emma stood there a moment longer. She was aware that the exhibit had smoothed things over, that there were probably whole libraries of detail she was not seeing, and she could not yet say why the electrons fell or what the protons were doing before they drifted in, and she was honest with herself about all of that. But she had one thing now that she had not had that morning, one solid stone to stand on.

"Okay," she said. "I have to redo my test answer. Oxygen isn't fuel. It's the final electron acceptor at the end of the chain in the inner membrane, and it picks up protons and becomes water." She paused. "I breathed that water. Some of the water in my body used to be air."

"That's either beautiful or disgusting," Priscilla said, hugging the plush mitochondrion.

"Both," Emma said. "It's both."

Josie dragged them toward the exit and the gift shop's second pass, and Emma touched her water bottle through her backpack strap, wondering which sip was newest.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Eye-contact norms differ: steady eye contact often signals confidence in North American interviews, while in some East Asian settings prolonged direct gaze at a senior person can seem impolite.
story:
The playground behind the elementary school had been Jeremy's territory since he was six, and it still worked for this: two swings, a climbing dome, a picnic table under the arboreal shade of an oak that the county had never gotten around to trimming. He sat on the table part with his feet on the bench, a printed job application folded into quarters in his pocket, waiting for Miguel and Mckayla to arrive so the pretending could begin.

The interview was Thursday. The hardware store on Delmore Avenue wanted a Saturday stocker, minimum wage, and Jeremy wanted it with a specificity that embarrassed him: money for a bus pass, for the winter formal, for not having to ask his mother. The trouble was not the wanting. The trouble was the rehearsal, because his mother's mother and his father's mother had each taken it upon themselves to prepare him, and they had prepared him for different universes.

"You look the man in the eye," his maternal grandmother had said over Sunday dinner, tapping the table with two fingers. "Whole time. Firm handshake. Say yes sir, no sir. Steady eye contact shows confidence here, that's how it works in this country."

His paternal grandmother, visiting on video call from Seoul, had been just as certain. "When you speak to the manager, keep your gaze down a little," she had said in Korean, which Jeremy half understood and which his father translated. "Looking too long at a senior person, that can seem rude. Humble eyes."

He had spent a week trying to do both at once, which meant his eyes darted around like a startled bird's.

Miguel arrived first, coasting his bike into the rack by the fence, then Mckayla with two iced teas sweating in a plastic bag. They had agreed on the plan during lunch: Mckayla would play the manager because she actually worked at the library and knew how managers sounded. Miguel would watch and take notes, then they would swap.

"Jeremy Wang," Mckayla said, standing at the slide as if it were a reception desk. "Thanks for coming in. Why do you want to work at Delmore Hardware?"

Jeremy looked at her forehead, then the ground, then somewhere over her shoulder toward the oak. "I, um. I'm good with, like, organizing things. And I'm reliable."

Miguel held up a hand. "Stop. Your eyes are doing the thing again."

"I know." Jeremy sat down hard on a swing. "Here's the actual problem. My mom's mom says stare him down, my dad's mom says don't, and they're both absolutely sure, and I can't do opposite things at the same time."

Mckayla sipped her tea and thought about it the way she thought about everything, which was longer than most people could stand. "Okay but," she said, "what if they're both right? Like, not about the same place, but about different places. Your dad's mom is telling you how it works over there, and your mom's mom is telling you how it works here. They're describing two different sets of rules."

Jeremy dragged his sneaker through the wood chips. He had been treating the advice like arithmetic, where one answer cancels the other, instead of like directions, where both roads go somewhere. "So here, in the interview, steady eye contact reads as confidence," he said slowly. "And in some settings over there, holding a senior person's gaze too long reads as rude. It's not that one grandma's lying."

"It's that you have two grandmas," Miguel said, shrugging, as if this settled it.

The presentiment Jeremy had carried all week, a cold little certainty that he would humiliate himself Thursday, loosened its grip slightly. Not gone. He was honest with himself about that much: he still did not know how much eye contact was too much, where the line sat between confident and aggressive, and no one at the picnic table could tell him. But he could practice a middle thing. Look while he spoke. Look away briefly when he gathered a thought. Return.

They ran it again. Mckayla asked about his schedule, his strengths, a time he had handled a problem. Jeremy answered in full sentences, and when she asked why he wanted the job he did not say "like, organizing things"; he said he wanted to learn how a business ran from the stockroom up, and he said it looking at her, and Miguel pumped his fist without irony.

"One more," Mckayla said. "The curveball. Where do you see yourself in five years?"

Jeremy swung slowly, the chains creaking, and let the question sit. He could not see five years out. He could see Thursday, and the bus route to Delmore, and a Saturday apron with his name on a sticker. "Honestly, I don't know yet," he said. "I know I want to be good at whatever I'm doing. I figured this job would help me find out what that is."

Mckayla nodded once, the way she did when something had passed the library test. Miguel scribbled on his notepad and turned it around. He had written GOOD EYES at the top and underlined it twice, then drawn an arrow to a doodle of Jeremy shaking hands with a smiling hammer.

"Same time tomorrow?" Miguel asked, kicking the bike stand loose.

"Same time tomorrow," Jeremy said, and folded the application into a paper airplane, and sent it gliding under the oak.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: The three primary chords of a major key are built on its first, fourth and fifth notes, so in C major they are C, F and G.
story:
The music room smelled of valve oil and radiator dust, and the October light through the high windows fell in long bars across the staff paper on Isabella's stand. She had four days to finish a sixteen-bar melody for Ms. Visser's composition unit, and so far she had three bars, two of which she hated. The assignment required chord changes written in standard notation, which was the part that frightened her. She could sing a line all day; putting harmony underneath it, in ink, was another country.

Bianca slid into the seat beside her with her guitar case, which she carried everywhere although she could barely play it. "I've decided I'm doing the whole thing on three chords," Bianca said. "That's all I know anyway. My brother taught me. He says the three primary chords of a major key are built on the first, fourth and fifth notes, so in C major that's C, F and G." She counted them off on her fingers as though laying stones. "C, F, G. Sixteen bars, rotating. Done by Thursday."

"Visser will know it's a dodge," said Valentina from the piano bench, where she was picking out something jazzy and self-satisfied. "She'll say you historicized your own laziness. That's what she said about my essay on Gershwin."

"That's not even what historicize means," Bianca said.

"It is what it means when she says it."

Isabella wrote the three letters in the margin of her page, small, the way you write a phone number you don't trust yet. C, F, G. She had been circling the piano for a week looking for chords that were sophisticated, diminished things, borrowed things, chords with names like relatives from another town. It had not occurred to her that the plain ones at the beginning of the key might be load-bearing. That evening, alone in the practice room after the janitor had run the vacuum down the hall, she set her left hand on C and sang her three good bars over it. They sat. She moved her hand to F and sang the same bars, and they sat differently, sadder, like a chair by a different window. Then G, and the line wanted to move, to go somewhere, and for the first time in a week she wrote more than she crossed out.

By Wednesday she had sixteen bars. The melody was simple, almost embarrassingly so, four phrases that rose and fell like breath, the harmony moving C to F to G and home again in patterns she chose by ear and then checked against the staff paper until the ink agreed with her hands. She played it once through at the piano with the pedal down, and something about it snagged in her chest, a feeling of familiarity she took at first for pride. She wrote her name at the top and left it in Ms. Visser's folder.

On Friday Ms. Visser kept the class late to return the drafts. She moved down the rows slowly, and when she reached Isabella she did not hand the paper over. Instead she sat on the edge of the desk, which she only did when something was wrong or something was right, and Isabella could not tell which, and the room went very quiet in the way rooms do when everyone is listening to a conversation meant for one person.

"Where did you find this melody?" Ms. Visser asked. Her finger rested on the third phrase, bars nine through twelve, the one with the falling sixth that had snagged in Isabella's chest.

Isabella felt the heat climb her neck before she understood what she was being accused of, or rewarded for. "I wrote it. Tuesday night. It's mine." Her voice came out smaller than she intended. Around her, Valentina had turned on the bench, and Bianca's hand had stopped moving on the guitar strings.

"Play it for me," Ms. Visser said. "Now. From the top."

Isabella's hands shook going to the keys, and the first phrase sounded worse alone than it had in her head, thin and slow. She kept the chords simple, C under the opening, F pulling the second phrase down, G lifting the third. At bar nine her own voice nearly failed her, the falling sixth, and behind her she heard Bianca make a small involuntary sound, and she understood, all at once and in her body before her mind, that Bianca recognized it too. Her mother had a lullaby she'd sung when Isabella was small, before the divorce, something wordless in the kitchen, and Isabella had not thought of it in years, but her hands had known it all along, and so had Bianca's ears, because Bianca's mother and Isabella's mother had been friends, and the song had lived in both houses like a stray cat.

She finished the sixteenth bar and let the pedal up. The sound emptied out of the room. Ms. Visser was watching her with an expression Isabella could not read, and Valentina had turned back to the piano as if studying her own hands, and the radiator ticked twice in the silence.

"Bars nine to twelve," Ms. Visser said at last. "Whoever wrote them first, you wrote them second, and differently, and I can hear both things at once. The question isn't whether you stole it. The question is what you want to do about it now that you know."

Isabella looked at the page, at the falling sixth in her own careful ink, at the C, F and G written small in the margin where Bianca had first said them aloud. She put her hands back on the keys and played the third phrase again, slower, listening for where her mother's version ended and hers began, and the bell rang, and she kept playing.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: Kahlo painted The Two Fridas in 1939, the year she divorced the muralist Diego Rivera; they remarried the following year.
story:
Wyatt had printed The Two Fridas from the school library printer and taped it above his desk, and for three days he had looked at it the way Mr. Hernández had taught them to look: colour first, then composition, then symbol. He had a page of notes. Warm Frida on the right held a locket with a portrait of Diego; cool Frida on the left, dressed in white, held scissors and had cut her own vein, the blood dripping onto her skirt in deliberate red columns. He had written that the two figures formed a symmetry, that the stormy sky unified them, that the exposed hearts connected them like a circuit. He had written that it was a painting about being two people at once. He was proud of that line.

The assignment was due Monday, and the critique had to be five hundred words of formal analysis, no biography. That was the rule Mr. Hernández kept repeating. The painting must speak for itself, he had said, tapping the whiteboard with his marker until the cap cracked.

Kody came over Saturday afternoon with his own printout rolled up like a diploma and two cans of root beer, and they spread their pages across Wyatt's bed. Kody's notes were shorter but sharper. He pointed at the left Frida's bleeding artery and said, "This is the stronger figure. She's the one doing something to herself. The other one's just holding a picture."

"That's not fair," Wyatt said. "Holding the picture is doing something. She's holding him, and the vein runs between them. The blood starts because of the locket." He traced the thread with his finger on his printout. "It's one circulatory system. The composition is making an argument."

Kody drank his root beer and squinted at the image. "Or it's two arguments, and the painting can't decide."

That phrase stayed with Wyatt after Kody left. He sat at his desk that evening and tried to make the painting decide. He tested readings the way Sameer tested answers in calculus, by substitution: if the stormy sky meant turmoil, the Fridas became weather; if the white dress meant death, the blood became inevitable; if the blood meant vitality, the white dress became a lie. Each reading worked and each one erased the others. His five hundred words were starting to feel like they could reify a guess, turn a hunch into something solid-looking that was still only a hunch underneath.

His mother called up that dinner was ready, and he went down and ate without tasting much, and came back up.

He opened his laptop to check the image resolution and found a museum page. The gallery label was small, the type nearly decorative, and he leaned in. The Two Fridas, it read, 1939. He sat back. He had assumed it was earlier, from when things were fine, or ambiguous. He typed the date plus the painter's name into the search bar, half feeling like he was breaking the no-biography rule, half feeling like the painting itself had opened a door.

Sameer texted him at ten, asking if he'd finished the essay. Wyatt typed back, "Did you know she painted it in 1939? The year she divorced Diego Rivera." He waited, watching the ellipsis pulse. "They remarried the next year," Sameer replied. Wyatt read that twice. Divorce, then remarriage. The painting sat above him on the wall, both women holding hands, the vein uncut on one side and severed on the other.

Now the painting looked different, and this annoyed him, because the painting had not changed. The paint was the same paint. But the scissors had become harder to read as pure symbol, and the locket harder to read as pure composition, because the date insisted on standing in the room. He thought about Kody's line, two arguments that can't decide, and about the remarriage a year later, and how a painting made during a divorce could not have known about the remarriage, and yet here it was, holding both women's hands together anyway.

He deleted his favourite sentence. That hurt a little, the way it always hurt when a good line turned out to be the wrong one. He wrote instead about the horizon line, which was low and cold, and about how the warm Frida's dress was the only saturated colour in the lower half of the canvas. He wrote that the symmetry was imperfect, that the left figure dominated in tonal weight while the right figure dominated in colour temperature, and that the tension between them might be irresolvable on purpose. He stopped before he could claim it was. In the margin of his draft he wrote, unsure, and left it there, because he was.

Sunday, Kody texted a question about the stormy sky, and Wyatt typed the divorce dates into the reply, then deleted them, then sent them anyway. If his critique had changed because of the label, Kody's could too.

"You think that's allowed?" Kody wrote back. "Hernández said no biography."

"He said the painting has to speak for itself," Wyatt typed. "But maybe the date is part of what it says."

Kody didn't answer for a long time. Then: "Guess I'm rewriting."

Wyatt put the phone face down and looked up at the printout above his desk, at the small stitched heart and the larger one torn open, joined by a single thin artery, both women's eyes steady and unimpressed by his five hundred words. His mother knocked and said lights out soon. He said okay. He picked up his pen and crossed out one more sentence.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: The margin of error measures only random sampling error; it does not cover errors from badly worded questions, people refusing to answer, or poorly conducted interviews.
story:
The newspaper office smelled of toner and old coffee, and Levi had claimed the good chair by the window, where the afternoon light fell across the arboreal shade of the courtyard oak, its branches printing shadows on the layout table. He was supposed to be editing the sports pages. Instead he kept looking at the printout in Marius's hand, the one with the headline already set in bold: SEVENTY-TWO PERCENT OF STUDENTS FAVOR CUTTING THE ARTS BUDGET.

"Two hundred and forty responses," Marius said, tapping the number. "That's a real sample. And the margin of error is plus or minus six percent, so even at the low end it's sixty-six. That's a landslide."

Henry leaned over the printout from across the table. "What exactly did you ask them?"

Marius read from his phone. "'Given that the arts program costs the school money while producing no measurable results, do you support redirecting its budget to sports facilities?'"

"Come on," Henry said. "You might as well have asked, 'Given that Marius is always right, do you agree with Marius?'"

Levi laughed, but then he stopped, because Marius wasn't laughing. Marius was pointing at the number again, at the clean six percent, as if arithmetic could burnish a crooked question into an honest one. Levi had trusted numbers like that himself, all through statistics class, the tidy plus-or-minus that made a poll feel like a machine with tolerances, like something engineered. He'd never thought about what the machine couldn't measure.

"It's a real margin of error, though," Marius said. "I ran it twice."

"That's not what it's for," Levi said slowly, and even as he said it he was still assembling the thought, feeling his way along it. "The margin of error measures only random sampling error. That's all it covers. Your question being loaded isn't random. It isn't sampling at all."

Marius frowned at him. "It's the standard formula."

"Think about who answered, too," Henry said. "Who actually fills out a survey link at ten at night?"

Levi pulled the response file up on the office computer and they stood around it, three heads over one screen. Of the two hundred and forty respondents, more than half were on a team roster Marius had imported when he built his contact list, and the drama and orchestra mailing lists, which Levi found in the folder Ms. Banerjee kept for the paper's sources, had never been sent the survey at all. There was also a column of non-responses, people who had opened the link and closed it. Fifty-one of them. Nobody had counted the refusals as part of anything.

"Sixty-six percent of people who already agreed with you," Levi said. "That's not a poll of the school. That's a poll of your group chat." He said it without triumph, because he could remember doing something smaller and uglier himself, a cafeteria survey freshman year about lunch periods, where he'd stood at one door of the cafeteria only and then announced that everyone wanted later lunches. He'd been so pleased with his clipboard. He had never once wondered who walked out the other door.

Ms. Banerjee came in with her keys and a stack of proofs, saw the headline upside down on the table, and stopped. "That's going out Wednesday?"

"With a six percent margin of error," Marius said, and there was defensiveness in it, a last wall.

She looked at Levi instead of at Marius, which Levi understood was a kindness, an offer to let the students settle it themselves. "Do you stand behind the number?"

Levi thought about how strange it was that he had wanted the headline to be wrong, had wanted it before he'd had any reason, and that the wanting had made him look until he found the flaws. He wondered whether wanting something to be false counted as bias too, whether you could ever clean your own glass completely. He didn't say any of that. He said, "Not as it is. The number is real, but it doesn't mean what the headline says it means."

Marius sat down hard in the second chair and rubbed his face. "So we kill the story."

"We could run the question," Henry said. "Run both questions. The one you asked and a clean one, side by side, and let people see what a loaded question does." He was already sketching a layout on the back of the proof, two boxes, the wording printed in full.

Levi watched Marius consider it. It would cost him something, printing his own mistake at full size, and there would be no recompense for it, no prize for honesty, just the exposure. But Marius was the one who had recruited respondents at eleven at night, who had cared enough to get two hundred and forty answers, and that stubbornness could point in a new direction as easily as an old one.

"Fine," Marius said finally. "But we also run the response rate. And who we emailed and who we didn't. All of it."

"That's the story," Levi said. "That's actually the story."

They stayed until the corridor outside went quiet, and the oak's shadow climbed the wall and let go of the window. Marius typed the new headline himself, deleted it, and typed it again: WHAT WE ASKED CHANGED WHAT YOU ANSWERED. He turned the monitor toward them.

"That one," he said.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: The treble clef is also called the G clef because its curl circles the second line of the staff, marking that line as the G above middle C.
story:
Vincent had cleared the kitchen table of everything except the staff paper, and by eleven on Saturday morning the paper was already losing the argument. He had written eight bars of a melody in pencil, played them against the chords he had worked out on the living room piano, and found that the melody belonged to a different, worse song than the one he could hear in his head. He pressed the pencil down until the graphite shone.

His mother passed through for coffee and paused at his shoulder long enough to eulogize his grandfather, who had played accordion in a wedding band for thirty years and had left behind a box of hand-copied sheet music, smelling faintly of mildew and beer, that Vincent had carried up from the basement last night. "He couldn't read a word of theory," she said. "He copied everything by ear and by hand." She rinsed her cup and left Vincent alone with the box.

The copies were strange and beautiful, dense with ink, and every page began with a treble clef drawn in a slightly different mood, sometimes fat and confident, sometimes thin, once in a slant that looked like the man had been in a hurry or in love. Vincent set one beside his own page and compared. His clefs were timid. He had been drawing them for years, a curl and a loop, without once asking why the shape was that shape.

He opened his phone and called Tanner, who answered mid-yawn. "Question," Vincent said. "When you draw a treble clef, where does the curl go?"

"Like, which line?"

"Does it circle a line? Or is it just decoration?"

Tanner was quiet for a second, and Vincent could hear him sitting up. "It's the G clef," Tanner said. "That's what my mom called it. The curl circles the second line."

Vincent looked at his grandfather's page again, then at his own. On his own sheet, he had drawn the curl low, wrapped loosely around the first line, the way he'd always done it, fast and unexamined, because nobody had ever failed him for it. He set the pencil point on the second line of his staff and drew the loop around it, slow this time, and felt something rearrange itself in his understanding, quiet as a chair being moved to a better spot in a room.

Because his old clefs had circled the first line, every note he had written sat one line off from what he'd been playing at the piano. The melody on the page and the melody in his hands had never been the same melody. He had spent the morning revising a song that only existed because of a mistake in a symbol, and the strangest part was that some of it was better than what he'd meant. Bar four, which he had been about to erase, landed on a note he would never have chosen on purpose, and against the chord it did something sly and canny, leaning outside the harmony and settling back in like a guest who knew exactly when to leave.

He tried to decide what to keep. He knew, from the arguments in his English class, the word for what he was circling: epistemology, the study of how you know what you know. Was the accidental version of the melody his if he hadn't intended it? His grandfather had copied whole songs by hand, misreading as he went maybe, and the wedding band had played those versions for decades, and brides had danced to them. Maybe authorship was less about intending and more about choosing, about looking at what landed on the page and saying yes to it on purpose, the way you said yes a second time to something you'd already agreed to by accident.

Vincent worked until two. He kept six of the accidental bars and rewrote the rest, and by the time the sixteen bars stood complete on the page, melody over chord symbols, he could play the whole thing through without stopping. There were places where the tune still wandered, and he underlined those measures in blue, not to fix them today but so that future Vincent would know past Vincent had heard the problem and left it standing, honestly, rather than papering over it.

Parsa came by in the afternoon with two sandwiches and sat at the piano bench while Vincent played the melody through, hands a little cold from holding the pencil. Parsa listened twice, chin on his fist, and said, "The fourth bar. Did you mean that?"

"No," Vincent said, and then, after the word had been out in the kitchen air for a moment, "Yes."
